entries.text: For WALL·E, Burtt cut sound-and-picture ‘character studies’ like audition tapes; animators then animated to them and sound and animation were refined back and forth, which made the robot feel more authentic.

source.title: Ben Burtt Special: WALL-E, The Definitive Interview

entries.text: For Crystal Skull’s magnetic and telekinetic effects, Burtt recorded a buzzing mercury-vapor lamp in the Skywalker parking lot, then slowed, reversed and layered it.

source.title: Sound Trek: The Audio Explorations of Ben Burtt

entries.text: Burtt plans like a scientist: he breaks a script into tasks, estimates how many effects it needs — say 800 — and divides by the days available to set himself a daily quota.

source.title: Definition, October 2024 (Ben Burtt interview by Trevor Hogg)

entries.text: West Side Story opens on demolition, and Rydstrom’s sound keeps it going off screen: the neighborhood is audibly being torn down in later scenes, so the film never has to show it again.

source.title: 189: Gary Rydstrom

entries.text: In West Side Story’s knife fight, Rydstrom kept the blade swishes high and sharp while the ambience stayed low beneath them — like a band arranger clearing space for a featured instrument.

source.title: 189: Gary Rydstrom

entries.text: To get from the rumble’s deaths to the upbeat ‘I Feel Pretty’, Rydstrom’s team stripped away natural sound and left only church bells, giving the audience a moment to absorb the loss.

source.title: 189: Gary Rydstrom

entries.text: Rydstrom treated West Side Story’s city backgrounds — horns, sirens, pedestrians, crying babies — as music in their own right, placing each with deliberate timing and pitch around the score.

source.title: Gary Rydstrom's Work on West Side Story Earns a 20th Academy Award Nomination

entries.text: Rydstrom built Ad Astra’s opening sound from dialogue spoken later by Tommy Lee Jones and Liv Tyler, looped and morphed into music and soundscape — so you subliminally hear Jones long before you see him.

source.title: Gary Rydstrom Offers an Inside Look at the Sound Design for Oscar-Nominated Ad Astra

entries.text: Murch maps sounds on a spectrum: speech is ‘encoded’ (violet), music is ‘embodied’ (red), and effects, footsteps and atmospheres fall between. A clear mix spreads its simultaneous layers across that spectrum instead of stacking several from one band.

source.title: Dense Clarity – Clear Density

entries.text: Worldizing: play the clean track through a speaker in a real space, record it from a distance on a second machine, then tuck that under the original. Murch likens it to shallow depth of field—sharp source, softened surroundings.

source.title: Dense Clarity – Clear Density

entries.text: On Mank, Klyce’s team mixed the film clean first, then split it into nine stems—two music, dialogue, loop group, ambience, hard effects, footsteps, props and optical noise—so each could get its own tailored ‘patina’ of age.

source.title: Mank sound interview

entries.text: Digital reverbs didn’t sell Mank’s old-theater sound, so Klyce’s team played the mix back on Skywalker’s hard-walled scoring stage, captured it with about a dozen mics from screen to back wall, then blended it into the rear surrounds.

source.title: Mank sound interview

entries.text: In The Killer, Klyce made metal the character’s sonic theme: guns, lockers, license plates, even the metal cup he drinks from to avoid prints, clinking against an airplane tray. A material palette can define a person.

source.title: Killer sound designer Ren Klyce thrives under the challenge of artistic constraints

entries.text: Klyce cuts The Killer between perspectives sonically: objective shots carry the voiceover, while the character’s POV shots drop it and slam between loud (often The Smiths) and quiet—Fincher’s ‘crazy loud/quiet thing’.

source.title: Killer sound designer Ren Klyce thrives under the challenge of artistic constraints

entries.text: In The Killer’s closing-kitchen scene, the room grows steadily quieter to build dread, and each time the kitchen door swings open it releases a burst of cooks’ chatter and music—what Klyce calls the escape hatch of her fear.

source.title: Killer sound designer Ren Klyce thrives under the challenge of artistic constraints

entries.text: Klyce on The Social Network: the first mixes were conservative. Fincher had the bar walla and the club music pushed over the dialogue so lines sit on the edge of intelligibility—the audience leans in, and the room feels real rather than ‘movie’.

source.title: Q&A With Ren Klyce, Sound Editor for The Social Network

entries.text: For The New World’s Jamestown arrival, Malick had Lievsay stop cutting sound to the picture edits. Wind, grass, footsteps and Wagner flowed as one ‘river of sound’, elements rising and sinking independently of the cuts.

source.title: Music, Sound and the Worlds in Between – A Skip Lievsay Interview (Part 1)

entries.text: Lievsay fully built the 20-second stillness after No Country’s car crash: far-off traffic, a distant dog, glass tinkling down at three separate moments. None of it came from a mic on set—each sound was chosen and placed.

source.title: Rain is sizzling bacon, cars are lions roaring: the art of sound in movies (Jordan Kisner, The Guardian)

entries.text: Audiences hear what they’re conditioned to hear: movie rain is often frying bacon, and layering lion roars into an engine gives a car menace. Choose sounds for what they evoke, not what made them.

source.title: Rain is sizzling bacon, cars are lions roaring: the art of sound in movies (Jordan Kisner, The Guardian)

entries.text: For I Am Legend’s deserted New York, Lievsay’s team scrubbed traffic and crowds from production (re-voicing scenes via ADR where they couldn’t) and rebuilt the city around nature reclaiming it—water from underground springs, crumbling buildings, wildlife.

source.title: Exclusive Interview with Skip Lievsay on I Am Legend

entries.text: Lievsay’s team built the I Am Legend creatures from recorded actors and animals, edited for hours into vocal types; temp mixes of each type for the director shaped how the creatures behaved and fed back into the CG design.

source.title: Exclusive Interview with Skip Lievsay on I Am Legend

entries.text: A teaching exercise Kroeber used: record one scene, then design it twice—once romantic, once ominous—using only sound effects. It proves how much mood lives in effects choices alone.

source.title: Ann Kroeber Special: A Pioneering Sound Woman

entries.text: Late in The Irishman mix, Gearty added a squib hit to the opening head-shot so the moment reads as a two-beat ‘da-dump’—gunshot, then impact—selling blood spatter that lands just after the shot.

source.title: Behind The Irishman’s Superbly Subtle Sound

entries.text: Recording nine period cars at Floyd Bennett Field, Gearty chased long idles and material an editor can cut, and checked backgrounds for anachronism—a 1950s muffler sounds nothing like a 1980s one.

source.title: Behind The Irishman’s Superbly Subtle Sound

entries.text: Aadahl keeps layer counts low: every extra layer tends to dilute the core sound’s punch and clarity, the way blending too many paint colours ends in muddy brown.

source.title: Erik Aadahl Special: Exclusive Interview

entries.text: Before reaching for a source, Aadahl ‘pre-auralizes’: he performs the rhythm and timing of the sound with his mouth, then builds or edits the real material to match that vocal sketch.

source.title: Erik Aadahl Special: Exclusive Interview

entries.text: When jet recordings made a broom flight sound fake, Aadahl concluded he had the wrong source and went skiing in Wrightwood to record it, getting the speed and natural Doppler he was after.

source.title: Erik Aadahl Special: Exclusive Interview

entries.text: To fight ‘Too Much Sound’ in action, Aadahl trims a whoosh short so a beat of silence lands before the impact, and pulls background washes out entirely so the hits read with precision.

source.title: Erik Aadahl Special: Exclusive Interview

entries.text: Aadahl’s tank for The Creator began as a car’s tyres singing across a serrated highway median, recorded at every speed; tremolo was added, then rhythmic deep metal clunks were layered in for close-ups.

source.title: Creating the ‘Vintage-Futuristic’ Sound of The Creator

entries.text: Aadahl ran The Creator’s robot voices through digital vocoders controlled over MIDI, kept as live processing all the way through the final mix so treatments could still be adjusted on the stage.

source.title: Creating the ‘Vintage-Futuristic’ Sound of The Creator

entries.text: For Alphie’s powers Aadahl’s team refused a computer-made tone; the build resolves into a recorded didgeridoo so the child’s magic feels spiritual and organic rather than synthetic.

source.title: The Creator” Oscar-Nominated Sound Team on Blending Retro-Futurism, Robot Monks, & the Didgeridoo

entries.text: For Godzilla, Aadahl’s team recorded with a Sanken CO-100K, which captures up to 100 kHz, then slowed the ultrasonic content down into hearing range—mining an ‘invisible universe’ for new textures.

source.title: Godzilla Sound Designers Erik Aadahl & Ethan Van der Ryn on Creature Language

entries.text: Aadahl’s visit to an anechoic chamber shaped A Quiet Place: with the world gone, you start hearing your own pulse and breath, so the film magnifies tiny bodily sounds until they feel huge.

source.title: The Sound Designers of ‘A Quiet Place’ Discuss the Power of Silence

entries.text: To ‘world-ize’ Godzilla, Van der Ryn’s team blasted processed roars through a big speaker array on the Warner Bros. backlot and re-recorded them from rooftops and inside cars, capturing real urban echo.

source.title: Godzilla Sound Designers Erik Aadahl & Ethan Van der Ryn on Creature Language

entries.text: Van der Ryn’s team renders Regan’s cochlear implant as ‘hearing as touch’: a low rumble. When she removes it, the track drops to true digital zero—used in only three scenes to bond the audience to her.

source.title: The Sound Designers of ‘A Quiet Place’ Discuss the Power of Silence

entries.text: Rather than spot the sequel with Krasinski first, Van der Ryn and Aadahl worked alone with the cut, then sent him finished scenes—hearing real sound beats imagining how it should play.

source.title: A Quiet Place: Part II had one sequence that totally blew away the sound editors

entries.text: A Quiet Place’s creature clicks avoided real echolocating animals, which sounded too familiar; instead Van der Ryn’s team zapped grapes with a stun gun, standing in for flesh, and slowed the zaps down.

source.title: A Quiet Place‘s Oscar-Nominated Sound Designers on Triggering our Brain’s Reptilian Fear Response

entries.text: Much of what makes a good explosion recording is the location it was recorded in.

source.title: Oppenheimer film sound interview

entries.text: King’s team built Trinity’s blast from eyewitness accounts that differed, merged into one composite: a hard, sharp crack with a long thundering tail rolling round the hills, plus the bunker and its contents shaking.

source.title: Oppenheimer film sound interview

entries.text: For Dunkirk’s Stuka siren, King’s team mounted a real electric siren inside a 30-gallon steel drum with clamped resonators, recorded it in the desert off reflecting hills, then pushed it with natural-sounding overload distortion.

source.title: Sound for Dunkirk

entries.text: For the trawler target-practice scene, King’s team shot metal plates with suppressed guns so only the impacts were heard, then placed each hit in a quiet gap to jolt the audience like the trapped soldiers.

source.title: Sound for Dunkirk

entries.text: King’s team didn’t match Inception’s slow-motion shots with slowed sound: they either ignored the speed change entirely or played sounds unrelated to the action.

source.title: Inception: Exclusive Interview with Richard King

entries.text: At Nolan’s suggestion, King’s team shifts the pitch of real-world sounds in Inception as the dreamers drop a level, so the roar inside a jet morphs into city traffic on entering the first dream.

source.title: Inception: Exclusive Interview with Richard King

entries.text: King’s team built Oppenheimer’s black-hole collapse from a reversed explosion swept hard with EQ and layered with crushing rock, giving the sense of an implosion that never ends.

source.title: 2 Twentieth-Century Giants, 1 Sound Designer: Inside the Explosive ‘Oppenheimer’ and Musical ‘Maestro

entries.text: In Maestro’s Ely Cathedral Mahler performance, King’s team dropped all background while the music played, then let the world return only after it ended—a pause, then applause.

source.title: 2 Twentieth-Century Giants, 1 Sound Designer: Inside the Explosive ‘Oppenheimer’ and Musical ‘Maestro

entries.text: King draws Oppenheimer’s spaces with contrast: Los Alamos gets wind, thunder and heavily reverbed distant birds and coyotes for openness, while the hearing room sits on a low, airless rumble.

source.title: Double Oscar Nominee Richard King Unveils the Aural Secrets of “Oppenheimer” and “Maestro

entries.text: King’s team made Oppenheimer’s recurring stamping-feet motif grow more oppressive as the bomb nears, voicing his rising panic; during the security hearing the room tone itself vibrates as the lawyer shouts at him.

source.title: Double Oscar Nominee Richard King Unveils the Aural Secrets of “Oppenheimer” and “Maestro

entries.text: For Need for Speed cinematics, Deenen’s team once sweetened engines with layered bears, pigs, tigers and leopards for emotion; by NFS Shift they had moved on to distortion and synth sweeteners riding on top of real car recordings.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: "Need For Speed" [Exclusive Interview]

entries.text: To capture car crashes for Need for Speed, Deenen’s team put an SM57 right at the point of impact, inside the collision itself, rather than relying only on safe distant perspectives.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: "Need For Speed" [Exclusive Interview]

entries.text: I often start from the smallest: one-inch stereo Radio Shack speakers at very low volume.

source.title: Charles Deenen on Sound Design for Games

entries.text: To fatten a sound, Deenen stacks two Renaissance Bass instances tuned to different frequencies so both sub and low-mids grow; on L1, he shortens release for more grit and lengthens it for a smoother result.

source.title: Charles Deenen on Sound Design for Games

entries.text: Never edit exactly “on the cut”.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Reader Questions

entries.text: Move the sound out of the picture, don’t just stop it.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Reader Questions

entries.text: Trailer triage: on the first watch, note only what grabs you and sound just those moments. On later passes add what serves story, pace or music, then strip out anything that is merely noise.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Reader Questions

entries.text: In trailers, Deenen retimes the edit to his sound’s rhythm in Pro Tools and hands the picture editor an OMF or edit list to conform, because editors cut better when inspired by the pacing of sound and music.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Reader Questions

entries.text: A practice drill Deenen recommends: rebuild a favourite sound using only five random library sounds, one per category, for several days running. To reverse-engineer a reference, study each frequency band and play it at half or quarter speed.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Reader Questions

entries.text: Stuck for an idea? Deenen suggests humming or singing the sound you imagine into a mic and processing that, browsing a library at random, or simply laying sounds against picture until something sparks.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Reader Questions

entries.text: To find the sweet spot on a car, sweep a small wind-protected lav around it in repeated identical moves while listening for more tone and less noise, and keep exhaust mics clear of the hottest, most turbulent air.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Reader Questions

entries.text: Deenen’s 100-whooshes method: fill 10–20 tracks with long continuous material, bus it to a few submixes loaded with Doppler, flangers and envelope filters, sidechain-duck the buses against each other, gate in hits at the peaks, then ride faders live and record take after take.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: 100 Whooshes in 2 Minutes

entries.text: Before booking a car-recording location, have someone rev a car about 50 feet away as a noise test, favour closed forest or private roads, find out how long the surface takes to dry after rain, and avoid quiet passes at peak bird and cricket hours.

source.title: Charles Deenen Special: Car Recording Guide

entries.text: Deenen describes how, for the Star Wars Battlefront trailers, Source Sound split Ben Burtt’s original sounds into tonal and noise layers, kept the tonal core and rebuilt the noise in higher fidelity, giving them control in a dense mix.

source.title: The Sound of the Star Wars Battlefront Trailers

entries.text: Deenen’s trailer mixes stay clean and punchy partly because every effect with hiss or noise runs through RX in real time; for mismatched dialogue he starts by using Ozone’s Matching EQ to match one line to another.

source.title: iZotope Masters Q&A Series, Part 1

entries.text: Deenen’s ‘bigganizing’ trick for explosions and guns: gain-clip a sound by around 20 dB, then run it through a de-crackler. The result feels huge and loud without audible distortion, which is all about perceived loudness.

source.title: Charles Deenen: Crafting Epic Sounds with Sonnox Plug-ins

entries.text: Deenen’s Need for Speed team recorded every car with no turbo fitted so turbos could be layered back in as upgrades, and drove each one on real roads to capture authentic gear shifts with all their sputters and grunts.

source.title: Interview: Charles Deenen

entries.text: Minto captures gameplay footage and tracklays it like a film first, ignoring engine limits entirely; only once the ideal is clear does he work out how to make the game deliver it.

source.title: Ben Minto Unplugged

entries.text: To keep a gun feeling like it’s in your own hands, Minto gives the weapon mechanism its own delicate, distinctive Foley layer, so the handling detail anchors the shot close to the player.

source.title: Ben Minto on Game Sound Design

entries.text: On Battlefield 4, Minto’s team at DICE took player Foley out of the HDR mix system so huge explosions could no longer cull your own footsteps, keeping a constant link between your character and the world.

source.title: Heard About: Battlefield 4

entries.text: Small personal details sell immersion: in Battlefield 4 a water sprinkler changes character when you stand beneath it, adding the sound of water striking your helmet.

source.title: Heard About: Battlefield 4

entries.text: Battlefront’s sounds weren’t bounced as final files; they were assembled at runtime from layers inside Frostbite, a workflow Minto likened to Max/MSP or Reaktor rather than a DAW, making them almost infinitely variable.

source.title: Game Audio: The sound of 'Star Wars: Battlefront

entries.text: To recreate blasters, Minto went to a guy-wire and struck it for that classic twang. He also slipped in Chewbacca’s Tarzan yell with a one-in-a-million chance of ever playing.

source.title: Ben Minto: Star Wars Battlefront sound design – 'We put a sound in with one in a million chance of it playing

entries.text: Wind alone didn’t make Hoth feel right, so Minto’s team layered in howling wapiti elk, a door creaking in a storm and the interior of a cave behind a frozen waterfall.

source.title: DICE Discusses Ambient Sounds In Upcoming Star Wars Battlefront

entries.text: Andersen first tried putting Limbo entirely in mono to evoke old film, but found it unengaging and not immersive; instead he distorted sounds and then re-widened them into an almost anti-phase spatial spread.

source.title: Heard About: Limbo

entries.text: Andersen ran everything in Limbo through an old tape machine, which glued the sounds into one family in the mix, and a spring reverb with its wet level at zero acted as a hardware filter, thinning sounds into something more generic.

source.title: Heard About: Limbo

entries.text: Andersen structured Limbo’s soundscape as a journey: it starts as fairly naturalistic forest and grows steadily more abstract, almost transcendent, as the game progresses.

source.title: Heard About: Limbo

entries.text: We had loud footsteps to tell the audience that the environment is really silent.

source.title: Creating Audio That Matters

entries.text: Andersen’s rule for Limbo: the more recognisable a sound was, the more he distorted it. Voices or animals carried such strong associations they would wreck the atmosphere, so they stayed out.

source.title: Creating Audio That Matters

entries.text: For Inside, Andersen played mostly synthesized material through a human skull fitted with transducers and recorded it with contact mics. The result sounded bad at first, but restoring that damaged audio gave it a unique creepy, cold signature.

source.title: Audio Design Deep Dive: Using a human skull to create the sounds of Inside

entries.text: Andersen’s team on Inside put a wired contact mic into a professional sword swallower’s stomach, recording internal body ambience and projecting sounds into it; a captured heartbeat became the metronome for the lineup puzzle.

source.title: The mad science behind Inside's soundtrack

entries.text: Andersen often imprints the spectral shape of traditional instruments onto non-instrumental sounds using convolution or match-EQ, letting the computer help orchestrate a soundscape.

source.title: Control & LIMBO composer Martin Stig Andersen finds beauty inside the darkness

entries.text: For Control’s supernatural Hiss, Andersen rubbed a friction mallet against the enclosure of an EMT plate reverb, grounding something otherworldly in a real physical source.

source.title: Control & LIMBO composer Martin Stig Andersen finds beauty inside the darkness

entries.text: For Inside’s environmental reverb, Andersen sampled a flagship 1980s Roland R-880 hardware reverb and ran it as convolution, and he conveys space more through apparent source size than reverb.

entries.text: Becker says the deafening concert that opens Sound of Metal is there for dynamics: it sets a loud baseline so the later silences register as a physical drop, the way relief floods in when pain suddenly stops.

source.title: Creating The Poetic Sci-Fi Sound Of 'Arrival

entries.text: For a subtly shifting atmosphere, Bellemare’s team chopped wind recordings into tiny fragments and intercut them with fragments of unrelated winds, then kept the result low in the mix so it was felt more than noticed.

source.title: Creating The Poetic Sci-Fi Sound Of 'Arrival

entries.text: In Arrival’s flashbacks, Bellemare’s team uses natural sound with no pitching or processing; instead sounds from the present bleed into the past and back, with gentle fader moves and light EQ tying the timelines together.

source.title: Creating The Poetic Sci-Fi Sound Of 'Arrival

entries.text: Bellemare’s team made the radios and comms devices in Arrival by playing dialogue through real speakers and re-recording it, rather than faking it with EQ or futz plug-ins.

source.title: Creating The Poetic Sci-Fi Sound Of 'Arrival

source.title: Creating The Poetic Sci-Fi Sound Of 'Arrival

source.title: Toy Story 3: Exclusive Interview with Tom Myers, Michael Semanick and Al Nelson

source.title: Bringing Stories to Life: An interview with Tom Myers about the sounds of Walt Disney Parks attractions

source.title: Behind the Subtle and Disturbing Sound of Apple TV+ series 'Severance

entries.text: During lurching camera moves in the finale, Ribicoff added waves of sub-bass tones timed to the motion, aiming for anxiety felt in the stomach underneath an already dense score.

source.title: Behind the Subtle and Disturbing Sound of Apple TV+ series 'Severance

source.title: Behind the Subtle and Disturbing Sound of Apple TV+ series 'Severance

entries.text: A reversed political speech sits buried under dialogue in Ribicoff’s Severance mix, felt rather than heard — part of a mix brief to keep everything as quiet as possible while each sound keeps its character.

source.title: Behind the Subtle and Disturbing Sound of Apple TV+ series 'Severance

entries.text: For singers with huge dynamic range, such as Hugh Jackman and Russell Crowe, Hayes put two lavs on each actor: one close to the mouth for quiet passages and one lower down to take the loud ones.

entries.text: Hayes matches the mic to the voice: one capsule for bass-heavy voices and chest placements, a brighter one for shrill voices or rigs in the hair and hats. On Guardians of the Galaxy, a cable ran through Bautista’s prosthetic scars.

source.title: In Conversation with Simon Hayes

entries.text: On the trailer for Dharma, Nair built the rain, thunder and reverb tails around the music’s tempo, establishing the trailer’s rhythm first and then fitting effects to the narrative.

source.title: Mixing / Sound Editing a Trailer

entries.text: For trailer effects, Nair avoids sounds heavy in the 2k-8k range: the more peaks around there, the faster the LEQ meter rises toward the 85 limit for an approved trailer.

source.title: Mixing / Sound Editing a Trailer

entries.text: Because trailer loudness is measured as an average, Nair says that if you need something loud, you need an equal amount of soft material before it.

source.title: Mixing / Sound Editing a Trailer

source.title: Mixing / Sound Editing a Trailer

entries.text: Nair keeps trailer ambience minimal unless a scene is meant to feel real without score, since a trailer has neither the time nor the aural space to establish it. He also avoids layering too many sounds for one aspect.

source.title: Mixing / Sound Editing a Trailer

entries.text: When unsure about an effect while editing a trailer, Nair keeps an alternative option muted underneath for the mix.

source.title: Mixing / Sound Editing a Trailer

entries.text: For a bigger trailer sound, Nair uses more low-frequency elements, fewer mids and more sounds in the surrounds, while making sure the mix stays balanced and not tilted toward the rear. He relied on multiband compression more than EQ.

entries.text: On Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen the score arrived fully separated, out to 60 channels, with orchestral elements split and percussion divided into high, mid and low, so Summers could remove elements where clarity demanded.

source.title: Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen's Audio Action: Part 3

source.title: Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen's Audio Action: Part 3

entries.text: Summers mixed against the composer team’s high-quality orchestral mock-ups early, learning where the score was thick and where effects could embellish it. When the real cue arrived, it only brought more clarity and transparency.

source.title: Transformers: Revenge of the Fallen's Audio Action: Part 3

entries.text: Mixing Avatar’s dialogue, Summers was sometimes asked by Cameron to raise lines more than the team’s instincts suggested, and to pan them a little more to center, so dialogue stayed audible even in a bad theater with a failed speaker.

entries.text: Johnson on Alice in Wonderland: London was kept deliberately bland and ‘normal’, while Underland got exotic birds, insects and frogs layered for depth. Each location had its own sound: a lush castle by waterfalls versus a battlefield with only stark, lonely wind.

source.title: Alice in Wonderland" - Exclusive Interview with Re-recording Mixer Tom Johnson

entries.text: For Alice’s 3D version Johnson pushed elements, even dialogue, into the surrounds and panned dialogue to the speaker’s position in frame. The same moves proved distracting in 2D, which got much less dialogue panning.

source.title: Alice in Wonderland" - Exclusive Interview with Re-recording Mixer Tom Johnson

entries.text: When Alice changes size, Johnson left her voice quality untouched so it wouldn’t distract from the performance. Instead the room reverb tightened when she was big and grew larger and more alive when she was small, and her big footsteps got deeper.

entries.text: Productions often reach the climactic moment having already brought ‘a freight train of sound.’ Boyes works against that: you can’t add a cannon to an already loud battle and simply make it louder.

source.title: Interview with Chris Boyes

entries.text: For Avatar’s big explosions, Boyes built the percussive attack by truncating the transient elements of favorite explosions on the Synclavier keyboard, playing them as a sharp attack with a quick decay, followed by a sonic wash.

source.title: Avatar

entries.text: For Avatar’s 3D mix, Boyes’s team chose only specific elements, like a passing bullet or an arrow, to move back to front, logging frame counts and performing pans frame by frame. Too much sonic information at once would detract.

source.title: Avatar

entries.text: For Avatar: The Way of Water’s creatures, Boyes started from marine animals including whales, added library tracks, and built a language that followed human rhythms to carry emotions from hope to anger.

entries.text: Semanick listens for a voice’s characteristics and features them. Pushing dialogue above normal conversational level exposes frequencies that don’t sound like the person in the room, so he EQs to warm them, and watches shouted lines, which go higher and harder.

source.title: Michael Semanick - Storytelling with Sound

entries.text: Semanick establishes a room’s reverb, then pulls it off as the camera tracks in or characters speak intimately. Pulling reverb and backgrounds down and out, rather than keeping everything up, draws the audience into the characters.

source.title: Michael Semanick - Storytelling with Sound

entries.text: In Incredibles 2’s newscast that follows the signal down the wire, Semanick passed the voice through different futzes for the broadcast booth, added static over radio waves, and room reverb that filled then narrowed as the camera moved, with splits on everything.

source.title: Michael Semanick - Storytelling with Sound

entries.text: For Mrs. Potato Head’s ghostly far-eye voice, Semanick copied her line, advanced it several frames, sent it to reverb, printed only the reverb return and reversed it so it preceded the dialogue. He then added delays and reverb to the original.

source.title: Creating Film Sound: an interview with Richard Beggs, pt.2

entries.text: Mid-battle in Children of Men, Beggs made the loud battle recede and pushed small pinpoint sounds forward, so the chickens are heard, inordinately loud, before they are seen. This subjective point of view is not realistic but works dramatically.

source.title: Creating Film Sound: an interview with Richard Beggs, pt.2

entries.text: Given, say, 12 prepared and cut elements in a scene, Beggs picks the two or three that best convey it, then drops the rest or pushes it so far back it is merely colour. Specific choices beat quantity.

source.title: Creating Film Sound: an interview with Richard Beggs, pt.2

entries.text: In Somewhere, Beggs made the two portentous low-frequency pulses as the Ferrari passes under viaducts from a manipulated bullwhip rush, and built the musical drone beneath the engine from multitrack elements of a song by Phoenix, the film’s band.

source.title: Creating Film Sound: an interview with Richard Beggs, pt.1

entries.text: Shatz chased trains around Portland for Paranoid Park, recordings he later used on Wendy and Lucy. He would stack five or six train sounds at once, one with an insistent horn and one with the approaching engine, to make them sound great and scary.

source.title: CREW: Steve McQueen, Kelly Reichardt and Gus Van Sant Share a Secret Weapon—Sound Design by Leslie Shatz

entries.text: For Immortals, Shatz plucked an upright bass, slowed it down and shifted its frequencies. In an arrow-shooting scene, that resonance builds until it reaches critical mass and you feel it in your body: loudness through resonance, not level.

source.title: Carol Sound Designer Leslie Shatz

entries.text: Shatz maps different sounds to the keys of a music keyboard and plays them at random while watching a scene; pressing harder plays louder. He feels a typewriter keyboard and mouse are on/off devices that strip out human expression.

source.title: Carol Sound Designer Leslie Shatz

source.title: Avatar: Fire and Ash': Breathing New Life Into The Sound of Pandora – with Gwendolyn Yates Whittle & Brent Burge

source.title: Avatar: Fire and Ash': Breathing New Life Into The Sound of Pandora – with Gwendolyn Yates Whittle & Brent Burge

entries.text: Before a team starts work, Rohde wants each member to explain what creativity means to them: rebellion, order, self-expression or a universal statement. A group that knows its members’ creative stances can collaborate far more intelligently.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde holds that seeing matters more than hand skill: anyone can learn to draw once they learn to truly observe. The craft starts in perception, not in the tool.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde treats knowledge as raw material, as real as paint or clay. He will read a book on almost any subject, because all knowledge connects and a designer can only shape what they know.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Online image results favour what is popular and photogenic, not what is typical. Search ‘Mayan pyramid’ and you mostly get Chichen Itza, an atypical example. Knowing the right terms, learned from reading, gets you better references.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Photos of Venice show bright, wide canals because that is where good pictures can be taken. The real city is dark, narrow and humid; sound echoes oddly and voices come through walls. Design from the media and you build the wrong place.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde notes that Imagineering sends mixed teams on field research: architects, writers, set designers, fabricators. Each discipline notices different things, so a group corrects the blind spots any one observer brings home.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A fractal keeps producing detail forever, and every layer is tempting. A creative team has to decide when to stop generating, so that one version can be measured and built. Planning takes over only after that point.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde bristles at ‘theme’ used as a verb, as if it were decoration stuck onto a surface. For him a theme is a noun: the underlying idea that organises every decision in a complex project.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A single word like ‘freedom’ is too vague to be a theme. A useful theme statement both gives a reason to act and sets a standard for judging the results, so the team can sense the project before it exists.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: To build a theme, Rohde asks three things: what values sit under this project, why they are the right choice, and how they can be expressed so both the makers and the audience understand them.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Top-down command is too slow for a big creative project, and nobody can predict the next order. A shared theme lets each contributor make their own decisions that still fit the whole.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Once a theme exists, Rohde says, nobody owns it. Team members needn’t personally believe its values, only commit to them for the project, which takes the ego and ownership friction out of collaboration.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde calls a big kickoff brainstorm a strategic mistake. Stories get made by two to six people; only once the theme and story are coherent should the team grow, because newcomers then join something with momentum.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde says every executive review of Animal Kingdom began with the park’s themes restated before any idea was shown. Reviewers judged each proposal against agreed principles, not personal taste.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: After proposing a theme, test it on hypothetical cases. If it keeps producing good answers, the team develops a useful bias: everyone starts spotting fitting opportunities without being told what is right.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Things are not what they are. They are what they can do.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde says magicians amaze us using perfectly ordinary physics; the magic lies in what we expected. Keep the audience feeling they half-know where things are going but can’t quite predict how.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde warns against simply asking people what they want and handing it over. Creative work should turn expectation around, delivering a surprise that seems perfect and inevitable afterwards.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A goal makes the ending predictable, and energy drops once people can see whether it will be reached, like fans leaving a decided game. A theme is open-ended: it guides from the start and keeps the team curious.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: For a Coachella stage, Rohde’s team first built a favela set that looked like immovable concrete, then transformed it several times. First make the audience believe nothing can change, then change it.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Logic is refutable. Metaphor is viral.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A simile (‘like a leopard’) invites the audience to weigh similarities and differences. A metaphor (‘the engine snarls and pounces’) lands before they can argue. Rohde uses metaphor to make an abstract theme concrete.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Once the Pandora theme was clear, Rohde’s job shifted from giving orders to editing. Designers stopped asking what to do; they showed him what they had already done and asked for critique.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde shows how theme works as a chain of likelihoods: a place about the value of nature implies organic landscape, eroded buildings, rough wooden doors, tarnished knobs. Anyone following the chain can invent a fitting chair unaided.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A good theme is predictable without being prescriptive: whatever it doesn’t rule out is probably fine. That turns every team member into a driver rather than a dozing passenger.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde admits he neglects emotional care, so he leaned on producers for it and took a different role: guarding the perimeter, absorbing political hits and running interference so the team’s stress wasn’t compounded by chaos.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde suggests replacing loaded words like ‘exciting’ or ‘elegant’ with nonsense pairs like maluma and takete, which only carry a feeling. Then flip it: if the project is takete, list how it could be maluma.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A plan, Rohde says, is only a theory based on what you know today, and tomorrow you’ll know more. You need one to start, it won’t survive contact, and each step forward needs a fresh one.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde keeps four questions in view while a project shifts: why must this be done, how will I know it’s finished, how does today relate to the original plan, and what must happen today.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Pursue the right expression, not the original one. If theme and purpose drive you rather than a fixed destination, what you stumble on may beat what you set out for.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: When the brief kept shifting, Rohde kept asking ‘What are we trying to do here?’ The answers evolved until he found the real theme: not adventure, but belonging.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde distinguishes co-laboration, working side by side toward a shared result, from ‘sub-laboration’, working for someone toward a conclusion already decided. Only the first produces outcomes nobody could have predicted.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde’s first Tree of Life sketch was a modest 40-foot banyan. As creative director he could have forced it back to his comfort zone; instead experts kept escalating it, and the final tree far outperformed his idea.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Model-shop carvers proposed sculpting animals in relief instead of Rohde’s timid incised lines. He feared the cost; they knew their craft and assured him the difference was negligible. Trust specialists on what their own craft costs.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A goal is a by-product of the motive. Lead by the theme rather than the target, so that a new opportunity isn’t squeezed into an opinion formed before any real work was done.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde made a habit of asking ‘Why is this a good idea, and how does it flow from the theme?’ before giving his view. Soon everyone interrogated each other, him included, and rationale preceded opinion.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: If you hold authority, you may have to beg colleagues to argue with you until they get used to it, and then accept living with the arguments.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A leader’s task is to multiply leaders.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde distrusts consensus: it is usually coerced by fear of exclusion, and merely announcing you want it frames disagreement as disloyal. Aim instead for a clear spread of opinion from advocacy to dissent.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: For the Avatar ride, Rohde wanted a mid-ride pause of stillness and darkness so the climax would land; his producer said it would feel broken. The compromise: slowing almost to a stop, with the creature’s breathing filling the moment.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde backed leaning arches over floating mountains because they seemed feasible. Engineering showed the arches were just as hard and costly. The cautious option isn’t automatically the cheap one; test it.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde separates three things: critique judges whether the work meets its goal, dissent questions the direction itself, and opposition just wants you to stop. Welcome the first two; make opponents work as hard as you.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: In ‘triadic negotiation’ nobody owns the idea; it is set aside as a third party and judged only on how well it serves the theme and intended effect, which keeps debate impersonal.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A key question for any proposal: what does it hinge on, and how will that central idea be protected as it passes through production? Also: why do you believe the audience will receive it as you intend?

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Dissent is a form of participation.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Facing an immovable deadline on the Guardians of the Galaxy ride, Rohde’s team designed the attraction around the schedule: every part had to stand alone with no cross-dependencies, and a list of what to cut was agreed before work began.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Because people filter what they tell bosses, leaders get the least reliable information. Rohde always took a sub-role on his projects where he reported to someone who reported to him.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: No” is a lazy answer.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde argues a creative project should not try to predict its outcome; each day should be a discovery. But to be genuinely unpredictable, you first have to know exactly what the predicted result would be.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: For Aulani, Rohde’s team pinned up rival resorts’ marketing images and removed every redundant cliché. What survived, the specific local people, became the theme. Delete the generic and see what remains.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde defines courage not as the absence of fear but as acting while afraid. The key, he says, is treating fear as a reaction rather than as a fact.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Our brains overweight vivid, painful outcomes. Rohde urges teams to judge risk with numbers, not emotion: how much pain, how likely, what cost. Otherwise survivable risks get vetoed.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Fear may be justified, but panic is not a strategy.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Creative work should be risky, not scary. Rohde says risk management exists not to block action but to answer one question: if this is where we must go, how do we get there safely?

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: A leader must make others unafraid, not just be unafraid. Fear lives in the unknown, so Rohde puts the duty to dispel it first on whoever knows the most.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: When Rohde stretched a designer into a far bigger role, he paired the assignment with concrete promises: mentoring, cover, extra staff if needed and plans for what might go wrong.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde calls managing by fear both a moral and a managerial error. Frightened people lie, hide or shut down, picking the fastest way out of fear rather than better work.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde observes that failure is often just nostalgia for the original plan. It sets new conditions for the next move, so play the ball where it lies.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Persistence doesn’t always mean rebuilding the same thing. Rohde notes the Everest story needs a yeti that seems alive, not that particular machine, so a different solution might serve it better.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: The answer to momentary failure is always to go back and address the motive.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: In big ensembles, failure rarely traces to one person, and neither does success. Where failure is dangerous to careers, Rohde says energy goes into finger-pointing; forgiveness keeps people looking forward.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: In Rohde’s one-pencil, one-sheet exercise, nobody claims the theme is impossible without more materials. A strong thematic motive, he argues, removes the perception of limitation entirely.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde says limitations are never the real problem. Trouble starts when a creative team lacks the power and autonomy to transform the limitations it has been given.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Don’t wait for full consensus before moving. Rohde pictures paradise as a noisy room of people arguing hard, and warns that critics will still be along for the ride.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: After passing through many hands, a project eventually needs focus. Rohde calls it freezing the equation: keep the concepts that matter, cut redundancy, drop what the crew can’t produce.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Keep noodling and you risk passing the point where the work had shape and meaning. Because creatives work on impulse, Rohde says knowing when to stop takes training.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: An elegant solution is easy to break. A clear statement is easy to muddle.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde is spellbound by shadow puppets: flat silhouettes and voices holding audiences all night. It cannot be simpler, yet it works, so any extra you add had better be worth it.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Passion drives work forward, but Rohde says dispassion tells you when it’s done. Early work defining theme gives an outside standard for judging with an innocent eye.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: The aim isn’t to know what the audience wants, Rohde says, but to empathize until you want it too. Delivering only what people ask for is merely a design service.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde says the real project is the one still running five years later. Audiences reveal how the work actually behaves, prompting a second wave of design after opening.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Rohde says to separate the pursuit of quality from rewards. Do your best work, absorbed in the present; if it is cancelled, you won’t wonder whether you were the cause.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Profit can be the reward of creative work, Rohde argues, never its motive. He notes that Blade Runner and The Iron Giant disappointed at the box office and endured.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Structure should follow the product, Rohde argues, not the reverse. An existing organization wants to persist, while a creative ensemble must evolve, because the problem only emerges once design begins.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: Be clear and then be generous.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: People struggle to start from nothing. Before a community painting, Rohde sketched one image he was willing to erase, just to spark conversation and build momentum.

source.title: Floating Mountains: The Art of Imagining the Impossible

entries.text: For Tenet’s inverted bullets, King didn’t just reverse a gunshot recording. He split the shot into its mechanical parts (action, firing, the bullet leaving the barrel, the impact) and played those ordinary sounds back in reverse order, so you can always tell where the bullet is.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: King’s team recorded Tenet’s gunfire with John Fasal and Eric Potter in a canyon walled on three sides. They set mics 100 to 200 yards from the guns to pick up the long, varied echoes and reverb tails that a real outdoor space gives you.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: For Tenet’s F50 hydrofoil racers, King’s recordist taped 12 to 15 mics around a boat’s deck in deck-coloured tape and recorded all day. The signature was a high cavitation whistle from the foils, resonating up the mast. Splashes and hull hits came from other boats, because the whistle masked everything.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: Tenet’s runaway 747 runs at full jet power for a long time, so King used shifts in perspective to break up the intensity: tyre skids as the plane turns, moments where the engines drop away or change colour, and a deeper, louder sound when the camera is underneath.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: King on Tenet’s highway chase: the cars, including a turbocharged BMW M5, were chosen partly for their sound. To sell the low camera angle, Eric Potter recorded small road details: bumps, lane changes, running onto the shoulder, a tyre hitting a manhole cover. Drifts and skids were recorded separately for processing.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: For Tenet’s inverted world, King kept literal reversal to a minimum. Wind was designed to feel like suction instead of gusts, and the seagulls were built to sound like an echo of real gulls. King’s team found early on that simply playing elements backwards didn’t feel strange or special enough.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: King’s team worldized much of Tenet. Fight blows, kicks and inverted explosions were played through a loudspeaker and re-recorded in corridors and rooms with interesting echo. King values the acoustic accidents this gives, which are hard to get from plugins.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: When King builds a first-pass effects track for a Nolan film, he works with the music turned off. He wants the sound field to stand on its own as a complete three-dimensional world. Effects and score are then traded off on the mix stage.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: The fast F50 boat dialogue in Tenet couldn’t all be replaced. Rizzo cut ADR together with the production lines, using EQ and processing to make the ADR sound like the actors’ radio mics so the two would match. The goal was clearer speech without leaving the scene’s context.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: Zenimation cuts between Disney films made decades apart. Mills used ambiences as glue through each episode. In the rain episode, he made long transitions and added extra rain, sometimes as a surround effect, to carry viewers between films from very different eras.

source.title: The Sound of Zenimation on Disney+

entries.text: Mixing Zenimation, Fluhr kept the older films narrow and centred, as they were originally mixed. He moved carefully between eras so the image never suddenly jumped to a wide format. He used several reverbs with long tails to hold onto sounds across transitions.

source.title: The Sound of Zenimation on Disney+

entries.text: Fluhr knew many Zenimation viewers listened on earbuds in bed, so he checked both the 5.1 and stereo mixes on headphones, which he never does for theatrical work. The streamer’s dialogue-based loudness spec was a challenge because the show has no dialogue.

source.title: The Sound of Zenimation on Disney+

entries.text: For the research-ship crash in Alien: Earth, every member of Gilmore’s team tried complex layered passes on the thrusters that keep firing once the ship is lodged in a building. What worked in the end was a few chopped-up rocket recordings. Gilmore’s point: pick one cool sound, not ten.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: In the crash aftermath of Alien: Earth, Gilmore started cuts with a single panicked woman before bringing up the crowd beds. One person freaking out is what motivates everyone else. Spotted call-outs layered on top gave the scene its texture.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: Inside the crashed ship in Alien: Earth, the backgrounds were steam, sparks and groans, which couldn’t all play at once. Gilmore scored them like music: each groan placed for a reason, steam blasts that half-sound like Xenomorphs, and muted sparks before a big one so it really scares.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: Noah Hawley wanted the tick in Alien: Earth to seem to laugh at its prey. Gilmore built its chittering laugh from dolphin sounds, and Nolan McNaughton recorded his own sucking sounds for the feeding.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: On Alien: Earth, no Xenomorph close-up got a single stock scream. Gilmore’s team rebuilt every appearance from base layers, with performances that ramp from something like a simmering tea kettle into a hero scream, so the creature reads as angry, plotting or toying with its prey.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: For Alien: Earth backgrounds, Gilmore used dense cricket recordings he’d made in Mississippi, manipulated until they no longer sounded like crickets. He had refused to reuse Romulus sounds on the series, as he’d refused to reuse 1979 sounds on Romulus.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: Gilmore’s team laid Alien: Earth lab backgrounds as room tone first, then dressed them with spotted call-and-response machines. In the transfer room, where Marcy feels safe, the backgrounds are slightly discordant to suggest something isn’t right.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: Approaching the crashed building in Alien: Earth, some sounds warn you what’s coming. At other points Gilmore’s team pulled everything out so you don’t know what’s next, which is why the Rottweiler barking when the tarp is pulled back lands so hard.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: On Alien: Earth, Davey managed sound against Jeff Russo’s score through frequency and texture: keep out of the bands the score occupies, and lean on density. He compares it to Smashing Pumpkins guitars, which you can turn down and they still sound massive.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: Davey used Neverland’s jungle backgrounds in Alien: Earth to map the island. Prettier birds play with the hybrid kids, harsher insects in Boy Kavalier’s spaces, and mysterious creature growls deeper inland. Some of it came from bird, wind and tree recordings he made on his honeymoon.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: On Alien: Earth, McNaughton built the internal mechanics of Morrow’s transforming arm from old recordings of a small plastic toy truck being rolled, flexed and moved. He liked its thick timbre.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: While camping in Sequoia National Forest, McNaughton recorded barbecue grills and the doors of bear-proof food lockers, with a mic placed right inside the locker. That material became source for the groans and moans of Alien: Earth’s destroyed ship.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: For Alien: Earth’s endless spark showers, McNaughton designed a palette of diverse, tumbling sounds with pitch movement: libraries of constants, swelly bits, one-off actions and big blasts. He weaved them together so the sparks never become one constant sound.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: For the crash crowds in Alien: Earth, McNaughton avoided wall-to-wall screaming. He cut single shouts or words fading in and out of camera perspective, using panning and reverb to place the listener in the space.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: The echolocation-like rumble of the ‘orchid’ creature in Alien: Earth is McNaughton’s own stomach growl, pitched down with its bass harmonics emphasised.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Earth

entries.text: Montaño says the Fast films live in the midrange. Impacts, guns, metal and glass can wear the audience out, so on F9 he managed them by pitching down, compressing, limiting and EQing, getting in and out of hits quickly, and leaving short breaks between them.

source.title: The Sound of F9: The Fast Saga

entries.text: In F9’s action sequences, Montaño’s mix goal is ‘get me to Mia’: clear the way for whoever is giving instructions and running the battlefield, so the audience knows where the good and bad guys are, then return to the mayhem.

source.title: The Sound of F9: The Fast Saga

entries.text: F9’s electromagnets are tonal by nature, and steady tones get lost under other sounds. Montaño needed fluctuation in them to cut through, gave each vehicle’s magnet its own flavour, and used addition by subtraction: hit the magnet, get out, let other things play, come back.

source.title: The Sound of F9: The Fast Saga

entries.text: For F9’s Atmos mix, Montaño says full-range surrounds matter so moving objects keep their low end instead of losing it to bass management. He moved vehicles before and after they appear on screen.

source.title: The Sound of F9: The Fast Saga

entries.text: Pre-dubbing F9’s dialogue, Taylor watches for sharpness. Shouted lines move from the chest into the throat, and the resulting harsh frequencies have to come out. The dialogue still has to be big enough to get through the cars and the score.

source.title: The Sound of F9: The Fast Saga

entries.text: On F9, Taylor and Frank Montaño share the console. While Montaño runs a long effects pass on the speakers, Taylor tweaks his own stems on headphones at the same time, then checks them on the big speakers afterwards.

source.title: The Sound of F9: The Fast Saga

entries.text: Files has trouble cutting without mixing. As he drops in a sound, he adds some panning and a bit of reverb right away, because that’s how he judges whether the sound will actually work.

source.title: Mix Magazine Sound for Film & TV 2022 - Sound Changes w/Will Files, Craig Henighan and Julian Slater

entries.text: Even when he has supervised and designed a film, Slater mostly takes the dialogue and music chair at the final mix instead of effects. He knows the effects already, and switching sides keeps him from being too attached to his own tracks.

source.title: Mix Magazine Sound for Film & TV 2022 - Sound Changes w/Will Files, Craig Henighan and Julian Slater

entries.text: Last Night in Soho needed Soho’s transformation from a daytime work district to drunken 2am chaos. Slater sent three recordists out with gear for a whole night to capture what they found, sounds you wouldn’t think to ask for.

source.title: Mix Magazine Sound for Film & TV 2022 - Sound Changes w/Will Files, Craig Henighan and Julian Slater

entries.text: For Greyhound, production mixer David Wyman put a mic on every actor who speaks, about 25 isolated tracks, plus the ship’s phones and loudspeakers. That way repeated orders and reactions could overlap naturally. In post, Minkler’s team mostly cut from the main five or six tracks.

source.title: The Sound of Greyhound with Michael Minkler

entries.text: Years before Greyhound, Minkler spent an hour lying in the nets on the bowsprit of a 440-foot clipper ship under pure sail at 22 knots, holding mics out over the bow wash. It was a rare chance to record a ship with no engine. That material, enhanced, went into Greyhound.

source.title: The Sound of Greyhound with Michael Minkler

entries.text: Greyhound’s backgrounds are only wind, water and turbines, so Minkler kept them changing with the story. Engine pitch rises and falls with speed orders, and the wind howls or drops as the captain walks in and out of the bridge.

source.title: The Sound of Greyhound with Michael Minkler

entries.text: Minkler sets his limiter threshold four or five dB below peak, where many mixers use about a quarter dB. On Greyhound he aimed for big and exciting without loud, so the audience never gets pushed out of the film.

source.title: The Sound of Greyhound with Michael Minkler

entries.text: Score plays through about 85 percent of Greyhound and uses a lot of low end. Minkler uses the sub sparingly, and to keep engines and guns distinct he keeps every element moving in level, frequency and position, so subtly that you don’t notice.

source.title: The Sound of Greyhound with Michael Minkler

entries.text: For the facehugger corridor in Alien: Romulus, Files’s team had built complex creature vocals placed in Atmos at different reverb depths. When they muted all of it and kept only body movement and a few details, everyone agreed the scene was much better.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Romulus - Moderated by Johnnie Burn

entries.text: After the chestburster’s scream in Alien: Romulus, Files cut all music and sound. On the next shot, of the ship heading for the station, he held the silence instead of bringing sound back in. The audience freezes because the convention has been broken.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Romulus - Moderated by Johnnie Burn

entries.text: Files mixed Alien: Romulus with layers of film saturation and distortion under everything, and the opening near-silence carries film hiss, not digital zero. Silence in space is suggested by rolling off the high frequencies, which audiences accept as silence.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Romulus - Moderated by Johnnie Burn

entries.text: To make Alien: Romulus dialogue sound like 1979, Paterson applied the film saturation to the voices too. He let loud lines physically distort, didn’t tame every sibilant, gave each space its own reverb, and leaned on distant perspectives, limiting himself to what 1979 tools could do.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Romulus - Moderated by Johnnie Burn

entries.text: In Alien: Romulus, the Corbelan launch plays with no music at all. Score comes in only once the ship stabilises, and the contrast makes it land. Paterson says that boldness of choices is what the original films’ mixes were built on.

source.title: The Sound of Alien: Romulus - Moderated by Johnnie Burn

entries.text: Ripley shoots wide and holds shots long. Wherever he could, Zipf accentuated foreground sounds in the wide shots, adding to the sense that we are observing or judging Tom and creating life outside the frame.

source.title: The Sound and Music of RIPLEY

entries.text: On Ripley, Zipf synced Foley tightly to the production sound so you can’t hear where one ends and the other begins. On long fixed shots he used perspective and room acoustics to mark each cut sonically.

source.title: The Sound and Music of RIPLEY

entries.text: For Ava Paige’s vehicle in Maze Runner: The Scorch Trials, Lee slowed a distant jet recording right down for a haunting approach, then added a degausser and a Reaktor-built sound with a tearing, air-distorted quality; Atmos’s full-range surrounds and bass management gave it looming size and rumble.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Maze Runner: Scorch Trials

entries.text: To make The Curious Case of Benjamin Button feel sparse and period, Klyce’s team had recordist Aaron Zeller gather ambiences in New Orleans swamps and rural spots far from city noise, then built the backgrounds from those clean, unmodern recordings.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Curious Case of Benjamin Button

entries.text: Instead of a loop group for the elderly Southern voices in Benjamin Button’s old folks’ home, Klyce sent recordist Aaron Zeller into real care homes with tiny mics hidden in his sunglasses, pretending to read a magazine while he captured the real background chatter.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Curious Case of Benjamin Button

entries.text: Recording jungle and baboons for The Hunger Games: Catching Fire while hiking in light, Peirson ran two stereo pairs pointed away from each other about 70 feet apart, using different microphone models so the same location yields two distinct-sounding, quad-style layers.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Hunger Games

entries.text: During Catching Fire, Peirson worked down the hall from the director and played works-in-progress several times a day with all music and dialogue muted, so the director heard only the effects and backgrounds being added.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Hunger Games

entries.text: In Catching Fire’s jungle, Peirson avoided hard ambience cuts: backgrounds sweep in up to six seconds before the next scene, and a constant canopy of leaf movement overhead runs throughout, unnoticed but adding an oppressive, claustrophobic presence.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Hunger Games

entries.text: On Dunkirk, production mixer Weingarten recorded every principal boat that had a working motor as sound effects, plus boots on sand and street and harbour rigging, and even handed a small Zoom recorder to the Spitfire pilots to ride inside the planes.

source.title: Oscar Podcast - Dunkirk - Location Recording

entries.text: For the schizophrenic episodes in The Soloist, Scarabosio’s team recorded a cello making notes, squeals and squawks, then processed them to sound deconstructed, mirroring the character’s mind sliding from normal to unravelling; city sounds were also shaped into rhythmic patterns.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Soloist

entries.text: In The Soloist’s tunnel scene, as Nathaniel starts playing the cello, Scarabosio’s team let the roar of passing traffic recede and turn into gentle waves, so the world sonically falls away around him.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Soloist

entries.text: With a tiny team on All Is Lost, Proctor and Steve Boeddeker split the work by world rather than by reel: Proctor took everything Redford’s character did (movement, breathing, handling the boat), avoiding overlap between editors.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of All is Lost

entries.text: For Baby Driver’s Tequila shootout, where gunshot muzzle flashes had to land on the music, production mixer Ellis fed timecode to the cameras, video assist, editorial and the lighting dimmer board, even as playback speeds changed on the fly.

source.title: Oscar Podcast - Baby Driver - Tequila Scene

entries.text: For the street battles in The Hunger Games: Mockingjay – Part 2, Peirson’s team recorded guns among urban buildings to capture slaps and echoes, and inside a warehouse at different spots for tighter versus more open interior perspectives.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Hunger Games: Mockingjay, Part 2

entries.text: The toxic oil trap in Mockingjay – Part 2 first sounded like waves and water, which felt soothing. Peirson added pitched fire elements and mud to give it weight, menace and danger.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Hunger Games: Mockingjay, Part 2

entries.text: In the quiet woods scenes before the music enters in the Hunger Games films, Peirson builds the space point by point: a tree creak placed here, a single bird there, another bird elsewhere.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Hunger Games: Mockingjay, Part 2

entries.text: On Tetro, Horner treated the opening minutes as a sound design overture: introducing the effects that will recur, like the light bulb inside the character’s head, so the audience learns that those sounds mean they are in his mind.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Tetro

entries.text: As Benny walks through Buenos Aires’s La Boca in Tetro, Horner placed a distant, ambiguous shout in the space (a fight or a street football game), giving the neighbourhood a faint edge of danger without spelling it out.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Tetro

entries.text: Horner found Tetro’s Buenos Aires scooter recordings cut through the mix like a knife, so he used them wherever he could to build tension around a dialogue moment, then release it.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Tetro

entries.text: For Transcendence’s Atmos mix, Porter asked the music editor for eight 7.1 stems (orchestra, percussion, harp/piano, high synth, low synth) and placed each in a different plane of the room, separating music from dialogue and effects.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Transcendence

entries.text: When Johnny Depp’s uploaded character speaks from within the walls in Transcendence, Porter used Atmos to spread the voice so it commands the whole room, a booming, godlike presence he found limited in 7.0.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Transcendence

entries.text: Empire of Light’s cinema was a pop-up set in a seafront tent. Wilson had it built on its own steels, not touching the tent frame, and had the glass doors fitted with thick acoustic office glass in rubber gaskets so wind vibration couldn’t travel through.

source.title: The Sound of Empire of Light

entries.text: Protecting Empire of Light’s quiet dialogue on location, Wilson lobbied catering to deal with food waste so seagulls wouldn’t roost on the set roof, and had loud period cars choreographed to pass away from important lines.

source.title: The Sound of Empire of Light

entries.text: Because the camera never leaves the cinema during Empire of Light’s riot, Wilson miked both inside and outside the glass, giving post control over how intelligible the skinheads shouting through it would be.

source.title: The Sound of Empire of Light

entries.text: For the riot in Empire of Light, Burdon muffled the skinheads’ voices through the glass with EQ and a touch of glass-like reverb, keeping them very muted even when they’re right at the glass, which made the moment more disturbing.

source.title: The Sound of Empire of Light

entries.text: In Empire of Light’s lobby scene, with no music, Burdon kept clean production dialogue and stepped the crowd back, weaving a handful of elements down to a hush at the key line, then expanding again as the drama moves on.

source.title: The Sound of Empire of Light

entries.text: For the cinematic finisher kills in God of War Ragnarök, Jimenez borrowed film mix logic: hard effects anchored in the center, with non-diegetic whooshes and viciousness coming from the rears and travelling rear-to-front, so a short linear gameplay moment plays like a movie.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: Jimenez built Garm, the largest creature in God of War Ragnarök, for 3D audio: footstep sounds are tagged to each of the four paws and other sounds fire from points along his physics-driven chain, so walking underneath him puts sound all around the player.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: For giant roars like the bear Björn in God of War Ragnarök, Jimenez layered quad, more tonal echo tails on top of the positioned roar, selling the fiction that the sound propagated so hard it bounced back from distant canyons. Big impacts likewise trigger the environment: trees shaking, foliage and snow rattling.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: Jimenez kept Ingrid, the talking sword in God of War Ragnarök, organic rather than digital: glass particles scattered on a bowed cymbal, recorded with a Sanken and slowed down for magic tinkle, plus ocarina and human whistles morphed together in Logic’s Alchemy to form her ‘voice’.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: For Atreus’s Sonic Arrow in God of War Ragnarök, Higa slingshotted bullet casings and paper clips in the desert, since objects that disturb the air whistle best. A whip crack recorded on the same trip became the hit-confirm transient, and ocarina tones gave the arrow a pitch players can pick out in battle.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: The energy core of the Sonic Arrow in God of War Ragnarök came from a warbly laser-bass synth patch: Higa simply EQ’d out all the synthetic high mids, leaving a smooth, chaotic motion layer he could build the arrow around.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: For the elegant Light Elf assassins in God of War Ragnarök, Higa’s team struck tuning forks and waved them past the mic, borrowing the lightsaber idea of a moving mic for natural Doppler, then pitched the takes way down in the sampler for slow, regal passbys.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: Bifrost powers in God of War Ragnarök are used by many enemies and cinematics, so Higa’s team recorded hydrophones in tubs and canteens, stretched the sloshing, added small glassy debris, then wrote a style guide with shared source and references so every designer pulled from the same library.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: In God of War Ragnarök, Previty sidechains ambience to the music’s RMS with very slow attack and release: as the score swells, the ambience drops in level and gets a high shelf cut, keeping its body but removing detail that would fight the notes. Combat states duck it further.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: Previty gives every cinematic in God of War Ragnarök its own custom ambience mix state, because much of what plays under cutscenes is the live in-game ambience. With the game’s single unbroken camera, a hard ambience change at a transition would break immersion.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: Previty on God of War Ragnarök’s eight-enemy fights: to stop them turning to mush, a per-frame system sorts enemies by threat: at most two sit in the high-priority bucket, while the rest are turned down and allowed to duck harder. You hear whoever is attacking you right now.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: Previty explains that God of War Ragnarök scales its multiband sidechaining to overall game loudness: in a quiet cavern the ambience never pumps, but the louder the game gets, the harder the real-time side chains work to clear space for story dialogue.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök

entries.text: For the Spark of the World in God of War Ragnarök, Previty split the area into an icy, glassy tonal palette on one side and rocky lava-fire on the other. The central light’s base tone is a library recording of a kids’ choir warming up, cleaned, slowed down and made more tonal.

source.title: The Sound of God of War Ragnarök
