entries.text: Since Dunkirk, Nolan’s home releases including Tenet carry the theatrical master. Rizzo says the only change is a level compensation for home surrounds, with no separate near-field remix.

source.title: The Sound of Tenet

entries.text: In The Bear’s kitchen, Giammaria builds backgrounds by asking what would really be happening at that time of day, say three hours before service with five people next door, then whether it serves the scene’s emotion. Notes get as granular as ‘fewer forks, more dishes.

source.title: The Sound of The Bear

entries.text: Giammaria treats boom and lavs on The Bear like a wet/dry blend: the boom stays in almost all the time, reinforced by lavs (auto-aligned by the dialogue editor) for the chaotic multi-actor kitchen scenes.

source.title: The Sound of The Bear

entries.text: For The Bear’s fork-throw, table-flip and car-crash sequence, Giammaria cut the low-end thumps that ate loudness rather than drop the whole episode 2dB to fit them. Most viewers watch on TVs without full-range speakers, so the midrange has to do the work.

source.title: The Sound of The Bear

entries.text: Giammaria tries to keep The Bear’s dynamics in check so viewers go from whispers to a car crash in 90 seconds without reaching for the remote. After the table hit he slowly backs down the screaming, watching average loudness.

source.title: The Sound of The Bear

entries.text: On The Bear, actors often change a take mid shouting-match, so their voices bleed into other actors’ mics and alts won’t match. Benjamin found RX could surprisingly peel one word off another, especially where one line ends on an S as another begins.

source.title: The Sound of The Bear

entries.text: For the car crash ending The Bear’s family dinner episode, Scott D. Smith had a mic inside the car and one outside. Benjamin cut Mikey’s screaming from the interior mic only, so the perspective came straight from production.

source.title: The Sound of The Bear

entries.text: With The Bear’s heavily improvised shouting matches, Smith asks the actors before rolling where they’ll take the scene. If he suspects it will get loud, he dials everything down and trusts post to recover quieter lines, rather than risk clipping.

source.title: The Sound of The Bear

entries.text: For The Bear’s dozen-person family dinner, Smith miked everyone, used plant mics, ran up to three boom operators plus two utilities, and sometimes hid mics in actors’ hair, working closely with hair and wardrobe.

source.title: The Sound of The Bear

entries.text: For long, quiet scenes on The Bear, Smith goes out of his way to get at least one take that can be boomed. Relying on lavs alone strips the perspective and life from the scene, and muffled lavs are a reason people turn on subtitles.

source.title: The Sound of The Bear

entries.text: The Social Network jump-cuts between two depositions, so Klyce gave each room its own dialogue reverb and room tone, one ‘woody’, one ‘glassy’. These ‘vertical edges’ let the audience know instantly where they are, however frenetic the editing.

source.title: The Sound and Music of "The Social Network" Panel

entries.text: For the Ruby Skye nightclub in The Social Network, Klyce’s team got the club’s 2003 playlist, then made several treatments of the chosen song: a bassy one, a distorted one and a piercing 2kHz one. Stacked together in the scene, the music worked like a sound effect.

source.title: The Sound and Music of "The Social Network" Panel

entries.text: Mixing the score on The Girl with the Dragon Tattoo, Klyce found a distorted growl in Reznor and Ross’s stems doing the job of Salander’s motorcycle. The options: tune the motorcycle to it, make both work, or drop the effect entirely.

source.title: The Music in Sound with Ren Klyce

entries.text: On the animated feature Luck, Rizzo made frequency decisions shot by shot: while the sparkly good-luck crystals occupy the extreme high end, he avoids leaning into flutes and cymbals in the score, and he’ll pull back just the drums so rumbles and explosions can fill the low end.

source.title: Mix Magazine Sound for Film & TV 2022 - Sound Design behind animated feature film “Luck

entries.text: For the NYPD helicopter’s tailspin in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier finale, Patrick took steady helicopter recordings and rode the fader up and down fast for a classic chop, while pitch-shifting up and down as it spirals toward the bridge.

source.title: The Sound for The Falcon and The Winter Soldier - Mix Sessions

entries.text: Recording at home on The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, Patrick used her Dyson vacuum, processed in various ways, as a core of Redwing’s jet sound, both for full-speed flight and its stealth mode. Kitchen gadgets and tools became the extra articulation for Sam’s new Wakandan suit.

source.title: The Sound for The Falcon and The Winter Soldier - Mix Sessions

entries.text: For Redwing’s chirps in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, Patrick played small ceramic water-filled bird whistles as if ‘talking’, then ran them through Soundtoys Crystallizer presets, giving beeps that still hint at a bird. Nia Hansen had suggested Crystallizer for widening sources.

source.title: The Sound for The Falcon and The Winter Soldier - Mix Sessions

entries.text: For Captain America’s shield in The Falcon and the Winter Soldier, Patrick started from the classic Marvel hit, reversed and lengthened the ring-outs for throws, and added pots, pans and baking sheets to feel heavier. John Walker’s fake shield used only the pots and pans, minus the Marvel layers.

source.title: The Sound for The Falcon and The Winter Soldier - Mix Sessions

entries.text: Mixing The Falcon and the Winter Soldier’s action, Wild goes shot by shot asking what story each shot needs, carving fast moments into the timeline. She insists you do the work yourself rather than hear a limiter doing the mix for you.

source.title: The Sound for The Falcon and The Winter Soldier - Mix Sessions

entries.text: For One Battle After Another’s early chase in beat-up stock vehicles, Scarabosio made the dynamics spatial as well as level-based: cutting inside a car brings its rattles into the surrounds, and cutting outside returns the sound to the screen, following the picture cut by cut.

source.title: The Sound of One Battle After Another

entries.text: For the car interiors on One Battle After Another, García generally used a dynamic mic at low gain, which captures the transients of rattling, maxed-out vehicles well.

source.title: The Sound of One Battle After Another

entries.text: On Arcane, Eliot Connors spent much of the show crunching transients through distortion and checking them on iPhones to see what would pop. In the mage scene he left a couple of frames of silence just before the staff strikes the ground, so the magic hits you in the chest.

source.title: The Sound & Music of Arcane: League of Legends

entries.text: Eliot Connors cut Arcane’s fight scenes with single, isolated sounds rather than stacks: the spear landing, the grenade clicking in from the side, Jinx’s chomper on the board. Layering, he found, creates mud and eats the frequencies the score needs, so one well-chosen sound per beat keeps both readable.

source.title: The Sound & Music of Arcane: League of Legends

entries.text: For the Firelights’ hoverboards in Arcane, Eliot Connors built a signature sound from flute recordings by a staff flautist, adding slapback delay so the flute echoes out of the tunnel. Each cut then got its own flavour: a high-pitched dirt bike, horses, mechanical clatter for the kickflips.

source.title: The Sound & Music of Arcane: League of Legends

entries.text: For Rio, the lizard-like creature in Arcane, Eliot Connors first did a sync pass with his own voice, then blended creature calls with seal vocals. Pitching the seal down gave it a small cry that makes the audience pity it, and he let its scaly movement carry moments more than the vocals.

source.title: The Sound & Music of Arcane: League of Legends

entries.text: To keep Arcane’s Zaun from repeating itself, Eliot Connors varied the steampunk palette per scene. For a distant wide view he took a signature machine gear beat, pitched it way down and added a canyon-style slapback, and he slipped odd one-offs (a crow, pitched crickets) into gaps in the dialogue.

source.title: The Sound & Music of Arcane: League of Legends

entries.text: Facing dense Arcane scenes, Eliot Connors cut one layer at a time: the boards one day, then mute them and do guns and ricochets, then bring everything back to cull. He pre-dubbed and panned before the stage so mixers could spend their time on dialogue, music and effects balance.

source.title: The Sound & Music of Arcane: League of Legends

entries.text: Arcane was designed and mixed with stereo and headphones as the main target, since much of its audience are gamers. Eliot Connors checked his design on multiple pairs of headphones and cheap speakers, and at very low volume, to make sure backgrounds and one-offs still brought the world alive.

source.title: The Sound & Music of Arcane: League of Legends

entries.text: For Arcane’s hextech magic, Brad Beaumont’s team built clean, pure tonal palettes that avoid sounding synthetic: soft synths layered into custom instruments, married to Eliot Connors’ wine-glass recordings to keep them grounded. They agreed tuning with the composer early, so the palette could be moved anywhere and still sit with the cues.

source.title: The Sound & Music of Arcane: League of Legends

entries.text: The Fighter’s punches came from about six realistic elements varied through each fight: purpose-recorded boxing gloves on bodies, hits on meat with and without bone, and celery stalks against leather pillows. Odin Benitez’s team cut different blends for body and face hits, then Myron Nettinga mixed passes for David O. Russell to choose from.

source.title: The Sound of The Fighter

entries.text: David O. Russell rejected anything that sounded like a Hollywood whoosh on The Fighter, so Odin Benitez drew stylised moments from the real environment instead: ringing mic feedback he caught echoing round an arena, slightly processed boxing bells, and blood rushing plus Mickey’s breath for the subjective corner moment.

source.title: The Sound of The Fighter

entries.text: Every crowd in The Fighter was replaced. Odin Benitez recorded a whole fight night at the Home Depot Center over four to six hours, as tiny undercard audiences grew into the main-event crowd, with two roaming recordists. A borrowed recorder also captured the broadcast feed from ringside, corner and crowd mics.

source.title: The Sound of The Fighter

entries.text: On The Fighter, Odin Benitez sometimes mixed a punch too loud, and David O. Russell heard that as leading the audience. One of the last fixes on the major fight sequences was pulling the punches back, though some had to stay big enough to keep the energy up.

source.title: The Sound of The Fighter

entries.text: Library effects didn’t ring true for The Fighter’s Lowell neighbourhoods, so Odin Benitez’s team recorded their own: a real family argument for the crack-house scene, and a helicopter he caught hovering over his own house rather than any stock helicopter.

source.title: The Sound of The Fighter

entries.text: On a short schedule for The Fighter, Myron Nettinga pre-dubbed only the crowds, collapsing about 160 tracks into four or five 5.0 stems. Everything else stayed live on the console as automation, never printed, so ideas could still change during the final.

source.title: The Sound of The Fighter

entries.text: When the bell rings and Dickie pulls Mickey into the corner in The Fighter’s final bout, Myron Nettinga dropped the arena to a low, energetic ‘dither’ so the audience focuses on the brothers’ speech. Even the stylised camera-flash moments avoided whooshes.

source.title: The Sound of The Fighter

entries.text: In Woman of the Hour’s cold open, Paul Stanley’s team targeted winds for isolation, then let the cicadas ramp into an aggressive cacophony as the assault unfolds. Coyotes yip when they sense another predator, so that yipping is woven in more as the attack goes on and as it peters out.

source.title: The Sound of Woman of the Hour with Director Anna Kendrick

entries.text: Woman of the Hour’s opening was originally full of ambience. Tony Solis pared it back to near silence to teach the audience early that silence is intentional, not a QC error. When Rodney chases Sarah, Solis’s team dropped her distant screams entirely: seeing the struggle without hearing it feels more desolate.

source.title: The Sound of Woman of the Hour with Director Anna Kendrick

entries.text: For Woman of the Hour’s dating-show audience, Tony Solis worked through 48-plus tracks of loop group in three layers: call-outs, a specific murmur, and cheery reactions, each with its own reverb, moving in and out. Perspective followed the character: with Cheryl we hear her view of the stage; with Rodney, his.

source.title: The Sound of Woman of the Hour with Director Anna Kendrick

entries.text: Woman of the Hour’s Joshua Tree scene was fully ADR’d because of planes and wind, but Tony Solis kept the production performance and used only tiny ADR pieces to button sentences under aircraft. The effects mixers kept the centre channel clear, and ambience was just light wind, with cicadas only on the walk back.

source.title: The Sound of Woman of the Hour with Director Anna Kendrick

entries.text: Inside buildings on Andor, David Acord made sure a little of the exterior always bleeds in, whether a crowd or a speeder-by, so viewers stay geographically anchored on each planet. For Coruscant he reused Ben Burtt’s prequel-era backgrounds, peppered with new material.

source.title: The Sound of Andor - Season 1 with David Acord, Margit Pfeiffer and John Gilroy

entries.text: Andor’s Ferrix was a practical five-city-block set, and dozens of extras walking on crunchy gravel ruined the production tracks. Margit Pfeiffer’s team removed that noise, replaced and looped it, and filled the trading hub with a mix of languages and accents from across the galaxy.

source.title: The Sound of Andor - Season 1 with David Acord, Margit Pfeiffer and John Gilroy

entries.text: For Fred Hampton’s church rally in Judas and the Black Messiah, Skip Lievsay worked in stages. He first matched Daniel Kaluuya’s mics at different distances so the voice is continuous, then built production crowds, doubling takes and adding chants. He looped a short drum beat and filtered and reverbed the music track to match production.

source.title: Judas and the Black Messiah - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: The rally in Judas and the Black Messiah is about 80% production sound. Rich Bologna’s loop group mostly filled gaps, but he placed some group in the ceiling channels to make the church feel three-dimensional, and carved out some low mids so the dense tracks glued together without harshness.

source.title: Judas and the Black Messiah - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: Daniel Kaluuya swung from yelling to whispering during Judas and the Black Messiah’s rally speech, so Marlowe Taylor covered him with a live podium mic, a hidden plant and a boom, plus booms and XY pairs on the 350-person crowd. He also asked the director for a take where the crowd responds live.

source.title: Judas and the Black Messiah - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: For Diana and Steve’s reunion in Wonder Woman 1984, shot under a semi-spherical ceiling at London’s Royal College of Surgeons, Peter J. Devlin wanted acoustic foam but couldn’t touch the set. Instead he floated balloons up under the dome, right above the actors, to break up its unusual acoustic.

source.title: Wonder Woman 1984 - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: In Wonder Woman 1984’s playful mall opening, Gilbert Lake gave the effects a rhythm that pokes through Zimmer’s jaunty score at its builds and stops. He used the walls and ceiling of the room so Diana’s lasso and powers feel energetic beyond the screen.

source.title: Wonder Woman 1984 - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: Rather than ending on a battle, Wonder Woman 1984’s transmission-bunker climax builds a crescendo of wind, paper, the machine and flying wishes, then turns in an instant to a subtle performance with very little sound around it. Gilbert Lake describes it as a different kind of superhero payoff.

source.title: Wonder Woman 1984 - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: The kitchen sing-along of ‘Silly Games’ in Small Axe: Lovers Rock is all production sync, with small pitch fixes and barely any lifts from other takes, because ADR would kill the energy. James Harrison added a little group to the later party sing-along, only to widen the colours of the vocal range.

source.title: The Sound for Steve McQueen's Small Axe - Mix Sessions 2021

entries.text: For Barbie’s dance sequences, production mixer Nina Rice used in-ear monitors and radio mics planted in the performers’ hair to capture clean sync over choreography. It took collaboration with costume and makeup; the Ken beach sequence alone needed 18 radio mics.

source.title: The Sound of Barbie

entries.text: When K and Joi go up to the rooftop in the rain in Blade Runner 2049, the rain starts real, then Doug Hemphill shifts it into K’s head: delicate and romantic. When K gets the call from work, the real rain comes back, a change meant to be felt, not noticed.

source.title: Oscar Podcast - Blade Runner 2049 - Rain

entries.text: Mixing the Twenty Thousand Hertz podcast, Taylor’s team keeps a tight dynamic range so every beat survives being turned down. A listener poll showed about 90% listened on earbuds, so they mix for earbuds and avoid the bright, brittle top end that sounds fine only on studio monitors.

source.title: Dallas Taylor - Twenty Thousand Hertz Podcast & Defacto Sound

entries.text: Twenty Thousand Hertz is delivered at around -16 LUFS integrated, and Taylor’s team holds that number exactly. The ads are stitched in dynamically at different times, so any ad can be swapped across the whole show and still has to sit seamlessly.

source.title: Dallas Taylor - Twenty Thousand Hertz Podcast & Defacto Sound

entries.text: On Defacto Sound’s car spots, the hard part is giving the impression of dynamic range with almost none: hitting hard, then dropping quiet, while still landing on a -24 loudness spec. Taylor says to always decide the mix by where it will be heard.

source.title: Dallas Taylor - Twenty Thousand Hertz Podcast & Defacto Sound

entries.text: For remote podcast guests, Taylor’s team asks even seasoned sound people for a test sample first. In a pinch, they record straight from a phone’s own mic, using Voice Memos set to high quality or a dedicated recording app, with a call recorder running as backup, because the voice is what matters most.

source.title: Dallas Taylor - Twenty Thousand Hertz Podcast & Defacto Sound

entries.text: On True Grit, Lievsay played the voice-over narration across the left, center and right speakers while keeping on-screen dialogue in the center only. That separation gives the narration its own space, which matches where it comes from in the story.

source.title: The Sound of True Grit

entries.text: For True Grit’s courtroom scene, Lievsay started with a realistic, warm church-like reverb on the voices. As the camera pushed in on Rooster during the prosecutor’s attack, he made it louder and more reverberant, until it sounded like a preacher in a church: an effect people feel without noticing.

source.title: The Sound of True Grit

entries.text: Peter Kurland recorded True Grit with a boom plus radio mics on every take, and the dailies used a single mixed track. Lievsay and Byron Wilson went back to the isolated tracks line by line, since takes that sounded noisy in the mix often had one clean mic.

source.title: The Sound of True Grit

entries.text: No mics or cables were allowed near the horses for True Grit’s river crossing, so Lievsay’s team recorded horses in an equine hydrotherapy pool. The horses made almost no sound in the water except snorting to keep their noses clear. That snorting became the sound of the struggle.

source.title: The Sound of True Grit

entries.text: In True Grit’s night cabin standoff, Mattie’s footsteps on the roof were set at a level where the audience could hear them but the men inside plausibly couldn’t. On the mix stage, Lievsay added one loud wooden creak, then silence, to motivate the first shot fired up through the ceiling.

source.title: The Sound of True Grit

entries.text: Lievsay shaped voice quality to define the characters in True Grit. For Mattie, he made her voice slightly less deep so it read clearly as a young girl next to the gruff men.

source.title: The Sound of True Grit

entries.text: For True Grit’s back-room scene, Wilson didn’t re-dub whole sequences. Jeff Bridges came back two months later and re-recorded just the words “see you” of his last line, so individual phrases could be clarified. Some lines ended up half production, half ADR.

source.title: The Sound of True Grit

entries.text: To capture live vocals for the concert scenes in Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere, Maitland gave the performers earpieces, kept the speakers in front of them and the audience live. He shot the close-ups first, because Springsteen’s punishing register wore out Jeremy Allen White’s voice after about six takes.

source.title: The Sound and Music of Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere

entries.text: For a Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere phone call with Jimmy Iovine, Maitland recorded it live with a phone-line tap, putting the on-camera actor and the incoming caller on separate tracks. He asked the actors not to overlap, because one earpiece carries both voices at once.

source.title: The Sound and Music of Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere

entries.text: To keep the Colts Neck house silent for Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere, Maitland’s crew held all traffic and avoided airplanes. At the Stone Pony, by contrast, he put out as many ambient mics as he could, giving post separate room and speaker elements to blend.

source.title: The Sound and Music of Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere

entries.text: As Bruce drives faster and faster under “Frankie Teardrop” in Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere, Norris’s team put Soundtoys Decapitator on the engine, moving from dry to fully wet with the acceleration. Under the song, the distortion seemed to separate from the engine and pulled the audience inside his head.

source.title: The Sound and Music of Springsteen: Deliver Me From Nowhere

entries.text: Cleaning dialogue for Strange Negotiations, Villaflor left the steady car and room noise in. Noise is fine as long as it’s smooth rather than jumping in and out and the words are intelligible, especially when the subject’s voice is that distinctive.

source.title: The Sound of Strange Negotiations

entries.text: With only five days to mix Strange Negotiations, Villaflor first bulldozed a broad pass of the whole film to get something printed and confirm the emotional arc worked. Only then did he go back with the director for fine-tuning and experimental transitions.

source.title: The Sound of Strange Negotiations

entries.text: When Paul first breathes in spice in Dune, Doug Hemphill does a big frequency roll-off that pulls everything out at once. Bartlett then spun the ethereal elements around the room and added Bene Gesserit voices with spinning delays to disorient.

source.title: The Sound of DUNE with Director Denis Villeneuve and Sound Team - Featurette

entries.text: For Sound of Metal’s deaf community dinner, Bladh planted mics under the tables and stuck contact mics, on wireless packs, under the surfaces with art department putty to catch the plate banging and table knocking. Post later blended these with boom and Foley.

source.title: The Sound of Metal - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: Knowing Sound of Metal would mostly be watched at home, Becker’s team spent real time on a separate TV/streaming mix with its own dynamics. A film that opens extremely loud makes viewers turn down, and then they miss the quiet passages.

source.title: The Sound of Metal - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: For The United States vs. Billie Holiday, Hein’s team used Andra Day’s own voice as a sound design element, processed until it no longer sounded like her, inside the film’s emotional ambiences.

source.title: The United States vs. Billie Holiday - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: In The United States vs. Billie Holiday, Hein’s team prepped the early clubs with loop group and effects so the audience talks and yells over Billie, because she wasn’t famous yet. The crowds grow and quiet as her fame rises.

source.title: The United States vs. Billie Holiday - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: Mixing The United States vs. Billie Holiday, Berger left the overlapping dialogue raw. He gave each cramped backstage and hotel space its own reverb combination, and used director-guided loop group lines to make every room sound specific without stepping on the performances.

source.title: The United States vs. Billie Holiday - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: After the bunker collapse in All Quiet on the Western Front, Kruse dragged contact microphones through earth for a crunchy texture, then pitched it down into an almost avalanche-like effect.

source.title: The Sound & Music of All Quiet on the Western Front

entries.text: For Oppenheimer’s Trinity test, King drew on eyewitness accounts and the hum of period analog equipment to build tense anticipation. He then held silence for the roughly 40 seconds before the shockwave reached the bunker, though audiences expect to hear an explosion when they see it.

source.title: Exclusive behind the scenes featurette with the OPPENHEIMER Sound Team

entries.text: For the found-footage horror film Backrooms, Battaglia started the mix as if everything came from the camera mic, then as tension rose spilled sound design into the LCR, and only at the most intense moments opened up surrounds with camera bumps and surreal ambiences.

source.title: The Sound of Backrooms

entries.text: Backrooms has almost no ambience: no HVAC, no air. Battaglia kept only the buzzing fluorescent lights, positioned them around the Atmos field and added reverb so you feel the size of the empty room, creating an uncanny loneliness.

source.title: The Sound of Backrooms

entries.text: Battaglia describes how the buzzing lights in Backrooms were recorded by Umberto Corte using electromagnetic and contact mics, capturing tones and textures in the fixtures that you would not normally hear with a conventional microphone.

source.title: The Sound of Backrooms

entries.text: On Backrooms Battaglia’s team found the creature scarier through incidental sounds than through screams. A peg-leg footstep became the signature danger sound, sprinkled around the space and heard progressively clearer as the film goes on.

source.title: The Sound of Backrooms

entries.text: To keep the Backrooms creature from sounding like a generic troll or ogre, Battaglia auditioned camel vocalizations, pitched down from the start. Director Kane Parsons picked one immediately, recognizing a likeness to a Half-Life 2 zombie.

source.title: The Sound of Backrooms

entries.text: On Backrooms some takes allowed only the camera operator and actor in the room, with 360-degree moves on 14mm and 18mm lenses. Hetmer’s only option was a tiny shotgun mic mounted on the Steadicam.

source.title: The Sound of Backrooms

entries.text: To expand R5-D4’s vocal range for The Mandalorian Season 3, Collins bought a reissued ARP 2600 synth, the type Ben Burtt used, and worked classic techniques: sweeping tones, filtering and vocoding, to give the droid fear and comedic beats.

source.title: Behind the Sound of The Mandalorian (Season 3) & Obi-Wan Kenobi

entries.text: Baby Driver opens with the studio logo re-pitched by Slater so its ping rings out into an infinite reverb tail that becomes tinnitus, in the same key as the strings that follow; a car’s brake squeal, reverse-echoed in that key, then leads into the first song.

source.title: Conversations with Sound Artists: 2018 Oscars Edition

entries.text: For Baby Driver’s long single-take Harlem Shuffle walk, Ellis hid playback speakers behind garbage cans and plants, then killed the music for a few dialogue lines in the coffee shop, using thumpers so the actors kept the beat.

source.title: Conversations with Sound Artists: 2018 Oscars Edition

entries.text: For the amphibian man in The Shape of Water, Robitaille started from his own voice so the romantic lead felt humanoid, not alien, then added animal sweeteners, liquid-rolling gill sounds and a breathing layer from Guillermo del Toro: one channel that grew to 64 tracks.

source.title: Conversations with Sound Artists: 2018 Oscars Edition

entries.text: On tight TV and low-budget schedules, Benitez’s editors pre-dub in 7.1 or Atmos rooms using clip EQ and some clip gain, so mixers get ready-made packages. Caution: clip gain hits plug-ins before processing, unlike volume automation.

source.title: Sound Editing and Mixing: Comedy, Drama and In-Between - Mix Sessions 2021

entries.text: The Ultimate Playlist of Noise goes to absolute silence for a stretch, with no room tone at all. Benitez expected a QC note for a dropout, but it went through, because the silence is the story.

source.title: Sound Editing and Mixing: Comedy, Drama and In-Between - Mix Sessions 2021

entries.text: Benitez urges filmmakers to have the film’s own mixers do the near-field version, since that is how a film lives on, and he bought a high-end Atmos soundbar to hear how most viewers will experience the mix.

source.title: Sound Editing and Mixing: Comedy, Drama and In-Between - Mix Sessions 2021

entries.text: In the horror series Them, Schultz played scenes as stark reality until a trigger moment, when everything else would peel away into heavy sound design or strange music, leading into a jump scare.

source.title: Sound Editing and Mixing: Comedy, Drama and In-Between - Mix Sessions 2021

entries.text: Schultz’s recorder is laid out to print every deliverable he has ever been asked for in one pass: mono comp, stereo DME, mono dialogue and effects with stereo music. Clean labelling avoids QC kickbacks.

source.title: Sound Editing and Mixing: Comedy, Drama and In-Between - Mix Sessions 2021

entries.text: For Napoleon’s battles, shot on about 11 cameras with up to 500 extras, Bucher recorded in three layers: one operator on a stereo-plus-centre rig for the overall battle, four costumed boom operators hidden on set, and 10 to 12 small recorders on stunt performers.

source.title: The Sound of Napoleon

entries.text: For Napoleon and Josephine’s whispered scenes, Bucher secured a VFX budget to paint out booms so they could go inside the frame. The very close, quiet dialogue then contrasts hard with the enormous battles.

source.title: The Sound of Napoleon

entries.text: Before shooting Napoleon, Bucher tested lav positions in Joaquin Phoenix’s costume and sent the files to post to agree on the best placement, then added a second mic inside Napoleon’s hat, recording 32-bit float.

source.title: The Sound of Napoleon

entries.text: On Napoleon’s Austerlitz shoot, while Ridley Scott was busy filming cannon set-ups, Bucher took 100 to 200 extras 10 to 15 minutes from set to record crowd reactions, returning them when needed on camera.

source.title: The Sound of Napoleon

entries.text: Each day on Napoleon, Bucher sorted his wild tracks and atmospheres into folders on a shared cloud system so post and picture editorial could pull them, building a location library as the shoot progressed.

source.title: The Sound of Napoleon

entries.text: Harrison’s sound arc in Napoleon follows his strategic rise: musket and hand-to-hand sounds made for the skittish first battle at Toulon were dirty and chaotic, used only there, with later battles growing more well-oiled and structured.

source.title: The Sound of Napoleon

entries.text: For Napoleon’s coronation in a huge cathedral, Massey layered extra reverb on top of the production’s natural room sound and opened it into all four corners, so Napoleon’s voice fills the hall; Ridley Scott likes rich, reverberant spaces.

source.title: The Sound of Napoleon

entries.text: To capture live singing on Wicked’s Dancing Through Life, Hayes close-miked everything: two lavs, left and right, plus a boom as close as possible, so every head turn lands on a well-placed mic that sounds like a studio but keeps the effort of the performance.

source.title: WICKED Sound Show with Exclusive Scene Breakdowns

entries.text: Wicked’s What Is This Feeling had slamming desks, choreography and quick cuts. Hayes recorded the two leads’ live vocals as cleanly as possible and wild-tracked all the background action so post could rebuild it.

source.title: WICKED Sound Show with Exclusive Scene Breakdowns

entries.text: For Wicked’s musical numbers, regular loop group actors got lost in the rhythmic sections, so Nugent Title worked with the choreographer to cast real dancers, who learned the rhythms and performed syncopated crowd vocals with the music.

source.title: WICKED Sound Show with Exclusive Scene Breakdowns

entries.text: On Wicked, Marquis worked with click tracks from start to end of every reel, so effects in songs like Dancing Through Life could play with and against the music like another percussion instrument.

source.title: WICKED Sound Show with Exclusive Scene Breakdowns

entries.text: To give Oz a slightly strange flavour in Wicked, Marquis used a collection of gamelan instruments, metallic, mildly tuned tones, sprinkled through scenes, along with rhythmic, tuned effects in What Is This Feeling.

source.title: WICKED Sound Show with Exclusive Scene Breakdowns

entries.text: Ferrari shot with modern four-cylinder replica cars, so Lamberti’s team recorded the real period cars, including Nick Mason’s Maserati 250F, a Lancia D50 and a 1953 car standing in for the 315, raced hard on a UK track.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: Before the recordings, Lamberti, Michael Mann and stunt coordinator Robert Nagle spotted every race scene in Ferrari, including off-camera testing during dialogue: a downshift here, acceleration there. The real recordings then plugged straight in.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: In Ferrari’s Mille Miglia duel, Lamberti played the camera’s car, de Portago’s V12, as primary and, when cars ran side by side, panned the V12 and the Maserati’s throaty V8 hard left and right to clear space.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: Once the real Maserati recordings arrived for Ferrari, Lamberti and Andy Nelson found they carried so much power they did not need to be played very loud to feel powerful.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: Because the replica cars on Ferrari sounded wrong, Orloff chose mics to keep their engines out of the dialogue tracks so post could lay authentic engines underneath. He also had actors speak up as if over the period engines.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: For in-car dialogue on Ferrari’s race scenes, follow vans were often impractical at speed, so Orloff relied on recorders embedded in the cars, using RF where in range.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: For Ferrari’s rain-soaked dialogue by the car, Lee Orloff shot a wild take of the key lines without the rain machines. Weiser’s team used that clean track and put rain back on top.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: To make heavily accented performances clearer in Ferrari without ADR, Weiser’s team sometimes moved a single syllable a few frames within a word, keeping the actor’s own performance.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: On Ferrari, Weiser premixed selected ADR takes and put them in Michael Mann’s Avid alongside the original, so Mann could hear how it would sound and decide faster.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: In Ferrari’s church scene, intercut with a Maserati time trial, there was a close-up of one or two stopwatches. Nelson and Tony Lamberti added about 20 more, so the whole congregation seems to be timing the run.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: Ferrari’s opera scene begins offstage with the sound drifting through, then the full ambience of the hall; once on stage Nelson dried up the acoustic to make it intimate, which sets up the audience’s reflective flashbacks.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: Nelson and Tony Lamberti spent a lot of Ferrari’s mix in 7.1 and 5.1, so the Atmos mix never relied on choices that would fall apart in the formats most theatres play.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: At the Mille Miglia start in Ferrari, after cheering crowds, revving engines and Enzo’s pep talks, Nelson takes the track very quiet as Enzo walks away from the last driver, putting the audience inside his head.

source.title: The Sound of Ferrari

entries.text: For the addiction montage in The Social Dilemma, Gould noticed the iPhone unlock sound resembled a shotgun cocking, so he cut it on the documentary side and followed it with a punchy, shotgun-like impact on the Pinterest logo, later dialling back the ‘gunniness’ in the mix.

source.title: The Sound and Music of The Social Dilemma

entries.text: In The Social Dilemma’s quick-cut addiction sequence, Gould built a fly-through-the-eyeball whoosh from the Mac Mail ‘send’ sound, layered with notification sounds and a Formula One car pass to make it more dramatic.

source.title: The Sound and Music of The Social Dilemma

entries.text: For a shot of liquid rushing through veins in The Social Dilemma, Gould layered casino slot-machine dings to tie screen use to gambling, and pitched them to the music so they landed as a clean hit at the end of the phrase.

source.title: The Sound and Music of The Social Dilemma

entries.text: Gould pitched the AI server room tone in The Social Dilemma to clash with the score through the film, then retuned it to the key of the music’s final resolve when the code is rewritten and the room turns simpler and more natural.

source.title: The Sound and Music of The Social Dilemma

entries.text: The avatar in The Social Dilemma got a busy sound when it was a vague human shape, and Gould simplified it as the visuals sharpened until it vanished. For the AI’s last line he removed the vocal processing so the plain human voice landed as a contrast.

source.title: The Sound and Music of The Social Dilemma

entries.text: In The Invisible Man’s opening escape, Files’s team first played the waves loud to cover Cecilia’s sneaking, then reversed it: they pulled the waves out so she suddenly felt exposed. Files says nearly every mix decision followed her point of view.

source.title: The Sound of The Invisible Man

entries.text: At the bottom of the hill in The Invisible Man, the music drops from huge to quiet and odd crickets play, then cut out when Cecilia turns around. Files says it leaves it open whether someone is there or her focus shifted, and it makes the audience feel she’s alone.

source.title: The Sound of The Invisible Man

entries.text: For the camera-covered suit in The Invisible Man, Files’s team fed camera clicks and servos into the particle-based Sound Particles software, multiplied and randomised by the thousand, until it sounded almost insect-like. They used only tiny tastes of it when Cecilia senses something.

source.title: The Sound of The Invisible Man

entries.text: Files describes how, on The Invisible Man, P.K. Hooker ran room sounds such as a cricket through the invisible man’s suit-voice processing. When the camera settles on a spot, the faint warping hints that something stands between the sound and the lens.

source.title: The Sound of The Invisible Man

entries.text: Scenes in The Invisible Man with motion-control cameras and a green-suited performer had noisy production tracks, so Files’s team deleted them and rebuilt each scene from scratch. That gave them animation-style control to swap levers: big music, then effects, then everything out.

source.title: The Sound of The Invisible Man

entries.text: Files and composer Benjamin Wallfisch put The Invisible Man score into Atmos with ‘emotional panning’, swinging elements through the ceiling and rear so things swim around Cecilia’s head. They checked that the sense of movement through the audience still survived a 5.1 fold-down.

source.title: The Sound of The Invisible Man

entries.text: Files mixed The Invisible Man for contrast, like the quiet verses and loud choruses of a Pixies or Nirvana song. Sometimes the contrast came from level, sometimes from frequency, and often from stripping things away just before a big moment.

source.title: The Sound of The Invisible Man

entries.text: For the restaurant killing in The Invisible Man, Hooker’s team changed nothing in the mix when the throat is cut. There’s no sting, the music keeps playing, and the sound only starts to change as Cecilia takes in what happened.

source.title: The Sound of The Invisible Man

entries.text: Joker: Folie à Deux was mixed in Atmos, but Van der Ryn’s team kept the animated cartoon opening vintage, front LCR only. The narrow image made the cut to the first full-Atmos Arkham corridor feel much bigger.

source.title: The Sound of Joker: Folie à Deux

entries.text: For Arkham in Joker: Folie à Deux, Aadahl and Van der Ryn recorded guerrilla-style on Alcatraz around the tourists, capturing cell doors and smeared, blurry echoes. They used the echoes for the corridors of E Block, the solitary-confinement wing, to set it apart from Lee’s block.

source.title: The Sound of Joker: Folie à Deux

entries.text: For the ‘I Love Rocky Road’ bar scene in Weird: The Al Yankovic Story, Gallagher recorded about 30 friends singing the song at a party. He ran around them with an iPhone stereo mic to get moving stereo, then layered it with loop group under Daniel Radcliffe.

source.title: The Sound of Weird: The Al Yankovic Story with Director Eric Appel

entries.text: In the LSD sequence of Weird: The Al Yankovic Story, Gallagher pitched the tonal industrial-shredder effects to the actual notes of the score. Because nothing clashed, the mixer could push the effects hard alongside a dense score.

source.title: The Sound of Weird: The Al Yankovic Story with Director Eric Appel

entries.text: At the peak of the loud LSD sequence in Weird: The Al Yankovic Story, Solis tried pulling a master fader all the way down as a test. Absolute silence worked better than the usual low drone or bed, and Solis’s team kept it.

source.title: The Sound of Weird: The Al Yankovic Story with Director Eric Appel

entries.text: Because the songs in Weird: The Al Yankovic Story were re-recorded with separate stems (even the accordion’s left and right hands), Solis placed them in Atmos to suit each venue. Drums came out of the PA in the dive bar, and the outdoor number stayed dry without going flat.

source.title: The Sound of Weird: The Al Yankovic Story with Director Eric Appel

entries.text: For a tape-rewind gag in Weird: The Al Yankovic Story, Gallagher found that reversing the film’s dialogue sounded bad, while reversed music worked. He layered a reversed copy of Al’s Nine Inch Nails-style parody ‘Germs’ under the effect.

source.title: The Sound of Weird: The Al Yankovic Story with Director Eric Appel

entries.text: On Nomadland, Seivers didn’t treat the environmental sound in the production tracks as a problem to scrub out. He avoided heavy noise reduction and EQ, kept some signal noise for its vérité feel, and Sergio Díaz designed winds that blended with the production sound.

source.title: The Sound of Nomadland

entries.text: On Nomadland, Seivers moved away from sending correlated sounds to the surrounds. He used decorrelated, discrete sounds that aren’t shared across channels, which builds immersion without drawing attention, and made the near-field mix and downmix come together quickly.

source.title: The Sound of Nomadland

entries.text: In Nomadland, interiors sat mostly up front while exteriors let wind, insects and cicadas spread around the room. Seivers says the surrounds were almost never a general bed; Sergio Díaz designed specific sounds for specific surround positions.

source.title: The Sound of Nomadland

entries.text: Díaz planned Nomadland’s design in three levels: the van interior kept prominent to stay close to Fern, layers of different winds for her journey, and deliberate silence, as when she wanders lost among the Badlands rocks.

source.title: The Sound of Nomadland

entries.text: On Nomadland, Seivers and Díaz delivered the film to the director in 30-minute sections, each a near-complete temp mix. By the final mix they could sit back, watch long stretches and make broad, audience-level decisions instead of fixing details.

source.title: The Sound of Nomadland

entries.text: For the crashed-plane scene in The Midnight Sky, Thom used the wind as cover for rhythmic metal tapping that is never seen on screen, which hints at the violence of the crash. The tapping stops dead when Augustine finds the sick man inside.

source.title: The Midnight Sky - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: In The Midnight Sky’s plane scene, Hiland’s team started big and wide outside, then pulled sound back as Augustine climbed in, so the audience had to lean in. Backgrounds were taken down and out to almost nothing until the gunshot brings the scene back.

source.title: The Midnight Sky - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: For the asteroid strike in The Midnight Sky, Thom’s team rolled large boulders down hills into various objects, then muffled the impacts outside the ship. The aim was a nod to soundless space: what the astronauts feel through their bodies and hear over comms.

source.title: The Midnight Sky - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: On The Midnight Sky spacewalk, Foley was recorded flat in case the director rejected the treatment, then muffled and made bass-heavy in post to suggest bone conduction. Thom admits the processing was simply a low-pass filter, and Thom’s team introduced the effect gently.

source.title: The Midnight Sky - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: When blood appears in the astronaut’s helmet in The Midnight Sky, Hiland’s team slowly faded out every ship hum and exterior sound until only her breathing inside the helmet was left, making the moment claustrophobic.

source.title: The Midnight Sky - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: Thom says George Clooney re-voicing the younger Augustine sounded odd, and pitch shifting and voice-alikes didn’t work either. In The Midnight Sky, Ethan Peck’s lines are an AI deep-learning blend of Peck’s and Clooney’s voices.

source.title: The Midnight Sky - Mix Presents Award Season 2021

entries.text: On Coup 53, Murch pre-mixed the composer’s 22 music stems against dialogue and effects in his Premiere picture timeline while he cut. A violin never fought a key line, so the final mixer mainly had to place the music in 5.1 and set overall levels.

source.title: The Role of Art and Technology with Walter Murch

entries.text: Murch questions panning dialogue to the rear across cuts, as in Roma’s bedroom scene, where off-screen voices come from behind. He finds that in a cut scene, dialogue kept centred is still heard as coming from the character, while music sources can be panned.

source.title: The Role of Art and Technology with Walter Murch

entries.text: On a William Kentridge series with very reverberant location audio, Murch tried the de-reverb tool built into Premiere and found it tunable enough to remove the ringing while keeping some natural room, an exception to his rule that fixes work only when you don’t need them.

source.title: The Role of Art and Technology with Walter Murch

entries.text: On Monarch: Legacy of Monsters, Ellis and Shaughnessy Hare check Godzilla’s footsteps and roars by feeling their own chests on the stage. She says that physical check translates to home viewing, and that big is easy while believable is the hard part.

source.title: The Sound of Monarch: Legacy of Monsters

entries.text: On TRON: Legacy’s light cycles, Boeddeker used ‘resonant sweeping’, borrowed from DJ filter sweeps: a resonant filter tracks the engine’s pitch as it passes, adding a high-tech whine. When a bike slowed to a stop, following the sweep down made it feed back on itself, and he kept the accident.

source.title: TRON: Legacy Sound Panel

entries.text: For the TRON: Legacy discs, Boeddeker built a pulsing tone so the Doppler would read as it flew. To give it movement, he played the tone through his design-room speakers and waved a handheld microphone in front of them, capturing natural acoustic motion as the basis of the sound.

source.title: TRON: Legacy Sound Panel

entries.text: For TRON: Legacy’s de-rez deaths, Boeddeker had the programs scream as they died so there was something to process: he automated in a ‘shuffle’ plug-in that particle-izes the voice, then added a crispy effect at the end to make it sound tiny.

source.title: TRON: Legacy Sound Panel

entries.text: In TRON: Legacy, the sound of a rider transforming into a light cycle, with tiles snapping together, came mainly from flipping through a deck of cards. Boeddeker noted that a deck of cards pushed into the subwoofer sounds really cool.

source.title: TRON: Legacy Sound Panel

entries.text: For a recurring kettle in Demonic, McNaughton recorded his own teapot and added a hydrophone to get a thicker low texture to blend in. He also recorded its switch on several mics at different perspectives so the moment it clicks off would land.

source.title: The Sound of Demonic with Director Neill Blomkamp

entries.text: For Demonic’s bird-like demon, Rossi first built a base vocal profile defining the shriek’s attack and release, then layered other material into it: cracking ice for crackle, shrieking metal for high accents and slimy gurgling goo holding the bottom end together.

source.title: The Sound of Demonic with Director Neill Blomkamp

entries.text: On Demonic, Rossi sent work-in-progress mixes of his creature to Foley, dialogue and the other sound designer about every two weeks. Everyone could see what he was covering, so they built complementary layers instead of duplicating sounds.

source.title: The Sound of Demonic with Director Neill Blomkamp

entries.text: For dialogue in Demonic’s first CG simulation scene, Renaud ran a delay through a flanger and spun it around the room in the Atmos/7.1 mix. Once the full mix was in you didn’t consciously hear the delay, only a sense of weirdness.

source.title: The Sound of Demonic with Director Neill Blomkamp

entries.text: Boyes recorded jungles worldwide for Avatar and warned about masking: a jungle works like an orchestra, and adding one or two elements too many breaks it. Building Pandora’s ambience was a careful balance of how many layers to let play.

source.title: Avatar Sound Panel

entries.text: Avatar’s viperwolves combined coyote pack-hunting yips, recorded in Malibu and in a sound editor’s backyard, with hyenas recorded at a UC Berkeley research facility. Boyes shaped them into a cross between a ferocious canine and a big cat.

source.title: Avatar Sound Panel

entries.text: Avatar was mixed in 2D, so the mixers, Summers among them, watched each reel in 3D with James Cameron, silent and close to the screen. Cameron called out what came off the screen, and they carried that spatial memory back to the stage to make sure those sounds came through.

source.title: Avatar Sound Panel

entries.text: Summers recalls that in Avatar’s thanator chase, James Cameron stopped the mix because he couldn’t hear Jake breathing under the roars and the music. Keeping the hero’s panicked breath audible kept the scene about the character rather than just a big monster sequence.

source.title: Avatar Sound Panel

entries.text: Thom made the explosions in How to Train Your Dragon deliberately heavy in low frequencies. That let them feel powerful and shake the whole environment without being ear-piercingly loud, which they would have to be if the intensity came from mids and highs.

source.title: How to Train Your Dragon Sound Show

entries.text: Thom’s team used ‘virtual pre-mixing’ on How to Train Your Dragon: every candidate effect sat in sync in a Pro Tools session, uncommitted, until the final mix. Since the final score often arrives on day one of the final, the effects could still be reshaped to fit the music.

source.title: How to Train Your Dragon Sound Show

entries.text: In dense battles like How to Train Your Dragon’s finale, Thom picks or builds sounds that change pitch over time, such as flybys and fire breaths. A pitch sweep grabs the ear in a way steady-state noise can’t, so it cuts through without just turning everything else down.

source.title: How to Train Your Dragon Sound Show

entries.text: Building the dragon voices for How to Train Your Dragon, Thom performed with his own voice to bridge gaps. He would mimic a tiger snarl closely enough to pass as the same creature, then steer it into a sympathetic beat a tiger can’t give you.

source.title: How to Train Your Dragon Sound Show

entries.text: For Toothless in How to Train Your Dragon, Thom and Al Nelson used horse breathing, including recordings of mares giving birth, for labored, emotional breaths. They pitch-shifted their own voices for the comic moments and used the subwoofer to make him sound bigger than he looks.

source.title: How to Train Your Dragon Sound Show

entries.text: For How to Train Your Dragon’s dragons, Nelson mixed animal vocals with non-animal sources such as squeaking styrofoam, rubber balloons, violins and slurpy liquids. A sea lion or walrus would be the base, and bowed metal or a squeak pushed it into a squeal.

source.title: How to Train Your Dragon Sound Show

entries.text: On How to Train Your Dragon, Rizzo found that Jay Baruchel’s unusually narrow frequency range needed more compression than expected to sit in the mix. Containing it let Hiccup’s voiceover cut through without getting too bitey.

source.title: How to Train Your Dragon Sound Show

entries.text: Under the How to Train Your Dragon opening voiceover, Rizzo moved the score’s brass out of the way while keeping the percussion. The narration stayed on top, the low-end explosions kept their weight and the pulse of the sequence never dropped.

source.title: How to Train Your Dragon Sound Show

entries.text: For the Owlship in Watchmen, Hecker layered jets and whines, then added a complex midrange synth tone run through an Eventide pitch plug-in. He mapped the pitch to a fader on a Command|8 so he could perform the rises and falls to picture.

source.title: Watchmen Sound Panel

entries.text: Dr. Manhattan’s subliminal presence in Watchmen was built from whale song, chosen over throat singing and waterphone for its natural chorusing and rising and falling pitch. Hecker’s team pitched, slowed and bent it per scene to track his arousal, anger and wonder.

source.title: Watchmen Sound Panel

entries.text: In Watchmen’s tenement fire, Hecker’s team pulled all the sounds inward, leaving a beat of silence just before the big explosion so it could land. The scene was otherwise so loud that creating ebb and flow was the main challenge.

source.title: Watchmen Sound Panel

entries.text: For WandaVision’s sitcom episodes, Dupre ran split stems of real period shows through a spectrum analyzer and matched their frequency response. Then she dropped the full TV-speaker sound, which pushed viewers away, in favor of an aged ambient noise bed and very sparse effects.

source.title: The Sound for WandaVision - Mix Sessions

entries.text: Dupre mixed WandaVision’s first episodes in mono, everything stacked in the center. Only subtle hints of a world outside the sitcom spread into stereo, until the episode 3 shift to color opened the mix into the surrounds.

source.title: The Sound for WandaVision - Mix Sessions

entries.text: For the WandaVision finale’s choking townspeople, Dupre layered the vocals through treatments that included compressors emulating constricting throats. Because of streaming loudness specs, she had to hold back the crowd build so Wanda’s magic still had room to be the big dynamic moment.

source.title: The Sound for WandaVision - Mix Sessions

entries.text: For WandaVision’s finale crowd, Foscato’s team went through three or four loop-group recording passes as the cut evolved. The first passes were too big and angry. The final version layered many subtle choking sounds and heavy breathing into a pad that didn’t intrude.

source.title: The Sound for WandaVision - Mix Sessions

entries.text: For Vision and the twins glitching apart in WandaVision, Orlando layered two different Dehumanizer presets, one glitchy, over the unprocessed voices. Dialogue could break up while the performances stayed intact.

source.title: The Sound for WandaVision - Mix Sessions

entries.text: To separate Agatha’s magic from Wanda’s in WandaVision, Orlando built it from the cicada sound in her lair, plus other insect buzzes and fire, avoiding Wanda’s sparkly tones. Agatha’s power-absorption effect started as literal water-sucking recordings, then processed.

source.title: The Sound for WandaVision - Mix Sessions

entries.text: For the station clocks in Hugo, Gearty found the real antique clocks he planned to record were all quartz-driven with no mechanisms left. Instead he recorded individual ticks from many sources and built each clock by repeating those ticks, giving every clock its own character.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Hugo

entries.text: On Hugo the boom was often swamped by set steam, so Stockton leaned on radio mics, de-crackled clothing noise and EQ’d out steam. When a lone line sat in a long quiet stretch, he ramped the noise up slowly into the line and back down, using visible steam bursts to justify it.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Hugo

entries.text: Scorsese loved Hugo’s automaton production track, which carried modern servo whine. Stockton cut it but kept it muted under Gearty’s designed mechanism, unmuting pieces only when asked, so the paper-scraping survived while the servo was notched out and used sparingly.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Hugo

entries.text: Hugo’s automaton-room dialogue was very noisy and the filmmakers refused to loop it. Fleischman’s fix: Eugene Gearty spotted small steam effects wherever steam appears on screen, so the noise in the production track reads as part of the scene.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Hugo

entries.text: In Hugo’s Méliès studio montage, Scorsese had Fleischman pull everything out of the track at the moment Méliès speaks to the boy, so one line of dialogue lands in sudden isolation inside an otherwise dense montage.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Hugo

entries.text: Mixing Hugo in 7.1 for its 3D release, Fleischman pulled the station inspector’s dialogue off the screen as his head pushes out toward the audience, matching the 3D image instead of leaving the voice locked to the center.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Hugo

entries.text: On Parenthood, with 14 regulars who improvise and paraphrase, Allen records every angle the same way, always capturing off-camera dialogue, with booms plus a wireless iso for every actor on a multitrack, so lines rarely need looping.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: Production Sound Mixer Nicholas Allen

entries.text: Allen chooses wire placement after watching rehearsal for physical business, such as hugging, carrying bags or turning in a car. He won’t EQ a voice unless placement colors it, and has his boom op keep wires clear of clothing so they match the boom’s sound.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: Production Sound Mixer Nicholas Allen

entries.text: On 42, when the loop group and production tracks lacked a crowd reaction, like the stands responding to Pee Wee Reese embracing Jackie Robinson, Johnson’s crew put up a mic on the dub stage, gathered everyone available, recorded it themselves and tripled it into the mix.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound and Music of 42

entries.text: Boeddeker’s first Tron: Legacy light-cycle sounds were purely synthetic. Adding Ducati motorcycle passbys gave them grit and weight, so he switched to real bikes heavily processed: doppler bys pitched far higher in and far lower out than natural, plus filter sweeps for a synthetic feel.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of TRON LEGACY

entries.text: Mixing Tron: Legacy in 7.1, Rizzo sold big arena spaces with delays, slaps and repeats travelling across the room. For intimate scenes he kept discrete ambiences and used different reverbs on dialogue in the front, sides and rear to define the space.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of TRON LEGACY

entries.text: Tron: Legacy’s light-up suits put a whine on all the production dialogue. Yates Whittle’s team cut it clean first, sent it for specialised spectral noise removal, then ran cleanup passes at the premix and again at the final, rescuing most of the production.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of TRON LEGACY

entries.text: For Smaug in The Hobbit, Boyes handled the growls, bellows, rumbles and fire breathing while Michael Hedges mixed Cumberbatch’s voice. Boyes interleaved them, so the growls emerge as the voice recedes and never step on a word.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of The Hobbit

entries.text: On Toy Story 3, Semanick used the new 7.1 side walls to ease dialogue just off the screen, slightly left or right, without putting voices on the back wall, creating better spaces for characters and music.

source.title: The Sound of “Toy Story 3

entries.text: Because Monsters University is a prequel, Myers didn’t reuse Monsters, Inc. technology sounds as-is: he took those ideas and degraded them, making them rougher and more low-tech for an earlier era.

source.title: The Sound of Monsters University

entries.text: For Monsters University’s campus, Myers’ team recorded ambience in the quad, cafeteria and stadium at Berkeley to capture college-campus enthusiasm, while watching that too much intelligible English didn’t creep into the backgrounds.

source.title: The Sound of Monsters University

entries.text: Pixar films pan dialogue more aggressively than live action, Myers says. Because the voice recordings are so clean, a voice can go wherever its character moves, with dialogue mixers adding perspective and reflections, as on Monsters University.

source.title: The Sound of Monsters University

entries.text: In Monsters University’s Toxicity Challenge, Myers put the loop-group crowds in the overhead and surround speakers. He removed a glow-urchin ambience because it muddied Randy Newman’s dense score, keeping only specific urchin flybys and stings.

source.title: The Sound of Monsters University

entries.text: Premixing Monsters University in Atmos with Gary Summers, Myers found that with many characters and busy music the screen piles up fast. Moving music and other elements slightly off screen cleaned up the on-screen dialogue.

source.title: The Sound of Monsters University

entries.text: For the Bat in The Dark Knight Rises, King started with helicopters. Ken Johnson then took the head off a weed whacker and fitted different things to spin, and processed versions became a major element. The final vehicle drew on about five ‘food groups’ of merged sounds.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound and Music of The Dark Knight Rises

entries.text: Bane’s mask hid Tom Hardy’s mouth, so King’s team on The Dark Knight Rises exaggerated the clarity of his voice. Early experiments added fluid through tubes, breathing and gaseous layers, but they made him harder to understand, so King’s team stripped them out and kept the voice largely natural.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound and Music of The Dark Knight Rises

entries.text: For Interstellar’s truck chase through the cornfield, King’s crew paid to mow down a real field with a pickup fitted with a metal bumper ‘corn catcher’, mics mounted behind it and inside the cab, driving repeated five-second runs.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Interstellar

entries.text: For Interstellar’s dust storms, one of King’s recordists built a sand gun, blasting gravel, sand and debris at an old junk truck; those hits combined with wind recordings sell the storm buffeting the vehicles.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Interstellar

entries.text: King on Interstellar: Nolan wanted production dialogue with almost no looping, only six to eight lines. Dialogue editors Hugo Weng and Bob Kaiser cut it like sound effects, dropping in syllables from other takes to articulate words better.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Interstellar

entries.text: For Interstellar’s ship shakes, King’s team put PA speakers and subwoofers in an aircraft-boneyard fuselage fed by two oscillators, running sine waves in and out of phase from below 15 Hz upward until the plane shook. It was the film’s only synthesized sound.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Interstellar

entries.text: King describes how Interstellar’s violent launch buffets needed character beyond a dropped aircraft wing, so Ken Johnson spent weeks recording a vibrating table loaded with metal to get layers of small rattles.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Interstellar

entries.text: Nolan banned hums, drones and bleeps from Interstellar’s spacecraft so it wouldn’t feel like Hollywood sci-fi. King’s ship interiors use the room tone recorded on set: the crew’s office, where they’ll live for years.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Interstellar

entries.text: Poppe scouted Need for Speed’s cars at car meets with an iPhone, judging rough samples on studio speakers. He then recorded each car in the quiet desert, ‘like a drum set’, with about ten mics on supercharger, intake, three or four on the muffler, sides and interior.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Need for Speed

entries.text: Recording Need for Speed’s cars, Poppe relied heavily on dynamic mics, which handle the sound pressure, and on omnis because they’re less wind-sensitive. Wind distortion was the one thing to avoid at all costs, since it ruins the signal.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Need for Speed

entries.text: For Terminator Salvation, Frankley banned servos and classic robot sounds. He recorded metal under stress, including metal slowly crushed in a log splitter, then processed those grinds to articulate the Terminators’ movements.

source.title: The Sound of Terminator Salvation

entries.text: For Terminator Salvation’s debris, Frankley ran a blower on a variac outside a stage, hosed into a tent inside, and blew sand and ground walnuts and almonds against metal, glass and canvas. Those were panned and traced through the winds.

source.title: The Sound of Terminator Salvation

entries.text: To give Terminator Salvation a family Skynet signature, Frankley ran much of the machine design through analog guitar pedals, including a ring-modulating wah, the Snarling Dogs Mold Spore.

source.title: The Sound of Terminator Salvation

entries.text: Terminator Salvation’s Moto-Terminators first sounded too slick. McG asked for Harleys, so Frankley recorded a Ducati and an MV Agusta with modified exhausts on a trailer-mounted dyno in the open desert, free of reflections.

source.title: The Sound of Terminator Salvation

entries.text: For The Last of Us’s clickers, blind infected who hunt by echolocation, Kovats and Derrick Espino workshopped vocals with actors until Misty Lee hit a tight, back-of-the-throat click. Kovats learned to emulate it and became the male clicker; heard unseen, echoing down a hallway, the benign click turns terrifying.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound and Music of The Last of Us

entries.text: Lanier describes how The Last of Us used an in-house ‘stochastic obstruction’ system: every game frame it threw out roughly 1,500 to 2,500 random raycasts purely for audio, spending a real chunk of the PS3’s Cell processor to model how walls and objects occlude sounds in its environments.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound and Music of The Last of Us

entries.text: On Brave, the first Atmos film, Rydstrom mixed traditionally in 7.1 first, then took the final-mixed material and turned individual sounds and dialogue lines into objects. Five screen channels instead of three let dialogue and effects panning across the front become far more specific.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Brave

entries.text: In Brave’s brawl among the Scottish lords, Rydstrom flung thrown men and sheep overhead as Atmos objects. Elsewhere King Fergus stands on a table while the triplets hide underneath; putting Fergus’s voice in the ceiling matched their point of view so naturally nobody notices.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Brave

entries.text: What first struck Rydstrom about Atmos on Brave was full-range, bass-managed surrounds: ambiences, door creaks, arrow-bys or dialogue moved behind the audience now sound as full as the screen. Even Brave’s unaltered 7.1 mix played better in the Atmos room for that reason alone.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Brave

entries.text: For the twinkling stars in The Little Prince, Nielsen rattled Goodwill glassware, light bulbs and chandeliers before recalling David Farmer’s obsidian chime recordings. He hunted down thin obsidian needles sold for Native American needlework and hung them as a mobile: part metallic, part glass, very pure, then manipulated them into every star sound.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Little Prince

entries.text: Because the Little Prince’s desert had to feel lonely and sparse, Nielsen built new winds out of paper, blurring Foley and effects; he and Foley artist Heikki Kossi spent weeks gathering every kind of paper to find what suited a world whose dunes are literally made of pages.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of The Little Prince

entries.text: Mission: Impossible – Ghost Protocol had loads of Russian dialogue shot with Czech actors. Yates Whittle had St. Petersburg-born Skywalker colleague Mika Makarov watch the whole film flagging accents and wrong phrasing for replacement, then brought him to Tom Cruise’s ADR sessions to coach his Russian.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound and Music of Mission: Impossible - Ghost Protocol

entries.text: For Ghost Protocol’s Burj Khalifa climb, Yates Whittle’s team salvaged production breaths and efforts, which are usually the first things lost. Scenes not shot on noisy IMAX cameras, like the hotel room, were cleanly recorded enough that much production dialogue survived into the final track.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound and Music of Mission: Impossible - Ghost Protocol

entries.text: For Avatar’s banshees, Boyes recorded two- and three-day-old piglets whose cries were unidentifiable; pitched down slightly with echo they turned birdlike, and he added guttural breathing from horses and assorted reptiles to build clucking, trilling calls and huge cries that carry across Pandora’s canyons.

source.title: The Sound of Avatar

entries.text: Building creature vocals on Avatar, Boyes gathers sounds from many animals like soup ingredients, then deliberately forgets their sources. He loads them into a patch on his synth and plays with how the elements fold in and out of each other, so no single animal reads.

source.title: The Sound of Avatar

entries.text: For Quicksilver in Avengers: Age of Ultron, who appears as a disturbance of air, Boyes created thousands of fast passbys with strong doppler but gave them agitation: rather than a smooth whoosh, a percussive, stuttering texture.

source.title: The Sound of The Avengers

entries.text: Wanting Ultron’s metal body to sound precise and metallic but never scrapey, Boyes found a tiny Burbank bearing supply shop, bought a large ball bearing and revolved it gyroscopically, producing about 100 tracks that he mixed together very subtly on the stage.

source.title: The Sound of The Avengers

entries.text: In Age of Ultron’s Atmos mix, Boyes valued bass management in the rear as well as the front: it adds power without making the track louder overall, used as Sokovia lifts into the sky and when grinding machinery starts up overhead as the heroes go underground.

source.title: The Sound of The Avengers

entries.text: Pain and Gain’s main title builds a sonic signature from recorded gym equipment: elliptical machines, dumbbells, clanking 45lb plates. Aadahl and Ethan Van der Ryn laid a Bumblebee vocal effort by late collaborator Mike Hopkins over a dumbbell clank as a tribute.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Pain and Gain

entries.text: For Argo’s revolution scenes, Aadahl brought in about a hundred extras to shout the exact Farsi slogans heard in 1979, placing mics behind windows, on rooftops, inside cars and in the middle of the crowd to capture each perspective.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of ARGO

entries.text: Archival footage showed 1979 Tehran used European two-tone sirens. Aadahl’s team built a car rig with two pneumatic two-tone horns, police and ambulance, and recordist P.K. Hooker drove it around the Warner Bros. lot to capture both close-ups and distant-city siren perspectives.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of ARGO

entries.text: For Inside Out’s memory orbs, which needed to feel glassy but sweet and musical, Mills’s team recorded different glasses filled with varying volumes of water to find the right pitches, then pitched them up and down, which became the sound of memories rewinding.

source.title: The Sound of Inside Out

entries.text: For Jurassic World’s gyrosphere, Nelson put a mic with a wireless transmitter inside a five-gallon glass carboy and spun it on a potter’s wheel, so no cable tangled. Rubbing wheels and objects along the outside captured glass resonance from inside, and he could vary the speed up and down.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Jurassic World

entries.text: For Lincoln, Burtt and recordist Greg Smith got into the White House with handheld recorders and recorded the French clocks that ticked during Lincoln’s presidency, plus the mahogany doors: knocks, hardware, keys turning and opening at various forces. Those are the doors and clocks heard in the film.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Lincoln

entries.text: Burtt describes how, to record Lincoln’s own pocket watch, wound for perhaps the first time in a century at the Kentucky Historical Society, Greg Smith built a small soundproof box holding the watch and a tiny Tram lavalier mic, closing the lid to isolate its ticking.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Lincoln

entries.text: With no recordings existing from 1865, Burtt rebuilt Lincoln’s soundscape from historical accounts: how busy the traffic was near the White House, whether steam trains ran and how far the yards were, which church bells could be heard. Then he gathered those sounds from museums and locations.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Lincoln

entries.text: Gravity’s handling and Foley sounds (loosening bolts, opening doors) were captured as transducer recordings of vibration rather than airborne sound. Lievsay says that whole layer split the difference between seeing an event and hearing it, and the reality that there’s no air in space.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Gravity

entries.text: On Gravity’s radio dialogue, Lievsay and Alfonso Cuarón found that the more futzed the voices, the more realistic but the less emotion reached the audience, so they kept adjusting the futz scene by scene, making it less literal when the moment needed feeling.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Gravity

entries.text: Lievsay’s mix of Gravity panned every voice with its actor wherever they floated, focusing the eye but also disorienting the audience. For Atmos, the essentially mono dialogue became objects carrying the 7.1 pans, then tracked even more precisely with added height.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Gravity

entries.text: Thom compares The Revenant’s bear vocals to directing an actor: his first pass let the bear overact, but Iñárritu wanted it to underplay, with empty spaces rather than a growl filling every moment of the several-minute attack.

source.title: The Sound of The Revenant

entries.text: Iñárritu’s made-up term ‘kakaya’ on The Revenant means offscreen noise you’d never design in, unrelated to the on-screen action yet believable for the location. Thom says it adds emotional resonance and realism, as long as it isn’t overused.

source.title: The Sound of The Revenant

entries.text: On The Revenant, Hernández pulled sounds from production dailies not for what was said but for their resonance and acoustics, then processed them to blend with the music, treating music as part of the sound design so viewers can’t tell where one ends.

source.title: The Sound of The Revenant

entries.text: To place Ratatouille in Paris subtly, Thom’s team recorded background voices with real French speakers, so straining your ears reveals genuine French murmuring behind the scenes.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Ratatouille

entries.text: In Scott Pilgrim vs. the World each fight has its own punch sound. The Matthew Patel fight uses 8-bit video game impacts, but true 8-bit punches sounded weak, so Slater’s team applied a pseudo 8-bit reduction while keeping weight so hits land in the gut.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection: The Sound of Scott Pilgrim vs. the World

entries.text: When building backgrounds, even a castle interior, Nielsen’s first move on Maleficent is to find the ‘air’: the overall feel of air and wind as a foundation. Then he adds offscreen life like people walking elsewhere in the castle, wind in trees, and strategically placed thunder.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Maleficent

entries.text: Maleficent’s recurring curse got its own voice treatment, sometimes intelligible words, sometimes an ethereal whisper; whenever it returns, Atmos let Nielsen move it through the overheads and to specific spots around the sides.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Maleficent

entries.text: Maleficent keeps its two worlds sonically apart: the Moors get exotic, unfamiliar birds and winds given tonal, magical qualities, while the human kingdom stays ordinary. Nielsen notes stage-shot fantasy films arrive with silence or fan and smoke-machine noise, so everything must be rebuilt.

source.title: SoundWorks Collection - The Sound of Maleficent
